articles.title: Meet Finley Holz, the Minnesota student who studied 10 years of wolf-tracking data and found deep snow can make wolves move less
articles.summary: US News: Holz combined wolf-tracking records with winter weather data, including temperature, snow depth and snowfall. Using ArcGIS Pro, he mapped wolf locatio.
articles.body: Holz combined wolf-tracking records with winter weather data, including temperature, snow depth and snowfall. Using ArcGIS Pro, he mapped wolf locations and converted them into movement data, while a Python programme helped compare movements with weather conditions. His research found that deeper snow was linked to reduced wolf movement. The study recorded a statistically significant negative correlation between snow depth and movement.However, cold snaps did not significantly affect how much the wolves moved. The research also produced an unexpected finding. Wolf movement decreased as a winter storm approached, while three days after a storm, movement was significantly below the average winter level. Holz's project was recognised in a Minnesota Story Map competition, where he placed second.How Finley Holz used wolf-tracking and winter weather data to study wolf movementHolz combined wolf-tracking information with winter weather measurements, including high and low temperatures, snow depth and snowfall events.The project used ArcGIS Pro to organise shapefiles and create maps showing wolf locations. The resulting location points were then converted into movement data. Holz also wrote a Python programme to align the wolf movements with the different winter weather conditions.The data came from wolf collar information provided by the Fond du Lac Resource Management Division. Pine Knot News, a Minnesota-based publication, reports that wildlife programme manager Michael Schrage provided wolf collar data and guidance to the students. Holz and other students also had the opportunity to collar Otter Creek wolf pups on the Fond du Lac Reservation on 5 May.Deep snow was linked to reduced wolf movement in MinnesotaOne of the clearest findings from Holz's research was the relationship between snow depth and wolf movement. According to the project published in Fairfolio, titled âThe Effect of Winter Weather Events on Wolf (Canis lupus) Movement on the Fond du Lac Reservationâ, Holz's second hypothesis was supported: wolves moved less as snow depth increased. The study found a statistically significant negative correlation between snow depth and wolf movement. In simple terms, the data showed that as the snow became deeper, the distance wolves travelled per movement decreased.The finding in similar terms, stating that Holz "found that winter cold snaps have no effect on wolf movement" but that there was "a negative correlation between snow depth and wolf movement: the deeper the snow, the less the wolves moved." Holz had also expected extreme cold to affect wolf movement. His third hypothesis predicted that wolves would move the least during a cold snap. However, the results did not support this idea. The Fairfolio project says there was no difference in wolf movement during a cold snap compared with normal winter movement. That meant that extremely cold periods, at least within the conditions examined in the study, did not produce the reduction in movement Holz had expected.Finley Holz found wolf movement decreased as winter storms approachedAnother unexpected finding came from the relationship between wolf movement and winter storms. Holz originally hypothesised that wolves would travel the furthest immediately after a storm. Instead, the data showed that their movement declined around the time of a storm.According to the project abstract, "Three days after the storm had passed, the wolves moved significantly less than the average winter movement (pFinley Holzâs wolf research earns second place in Minnesota Story Map competitionHolz's wolf research also became part of a successful Minnesota Story Map competition. Two Cloquet High School students and a Hermantown student with Cloquet connections won the top three places in the competition. Hermantown freshman Gabriel Bradley came first, while Cloquet sophomores Finley Holz and Melanie Buhs placed second and third.The Minnesota Alliance for Geographic Education competition challenges students to conduct research and present their findings through an ArcGIS Online story map.Holz's project focused on the effect of winter weather events on wolf movement, while Bradley's project examined factors affecting wolf pack den relocation.Minnesota studentâs decade-long wolf research reveals effects of snow and stormsHolz's project provides a detailed look at how winter conditions can influence wolf movement in northeastern Minnesota. Rather than finding that every form of severe winter weather caused wolves to travel less, the research showed a more specific pattern. Increasing snow depth was associated with reduced wolf movement, while cold snaps alone did not significantly change movement.The study also raised a new question about how wolves respond to approaching storms. The observation that movement decreased before a storm arrived suggests that further research could investigate whether wolves respond to changes in atmospheric or environmental conditions before severe weather reaches the area.For a high-school research project, Holz's work combined a decade of wildlife-tracking information with geographic mapping, weather data and computer analysis to examine the behaviour of an important northern predator.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'I was living paycheck to paychek': Woman says coming back to India from UK after 4 years not happiest decision but right one for nervous system
articles.summary: UK News: At a time when students outside India are in a fix to decide whether going back to India would be a better decision because of immigration bottlenecks.
articles.body: At a time when students outside India are in a fix to decide whether going back to India would be a better decision because of immigration bottlenecks, Arshiya Mahajan, an Indian woman shared her experience of coming back to India after living four years in the UK. Mahajan said it was not 100% the happiest decision she ever made but it felt like the right one for the nervous system as living in the UK was becoming a lot less living and more about maintaining a life, she said."Visa paperwork. Rental issues. Immigration timelines. Money. What happens when friends move away. What my next job should be. Whether I could actually afford the life I was living," she said, listing out the factors that worried her."I was living increasingly paycheck to paycheck, occasionally needing my family to help me out, while simultaneously trying to convince myself that I was âdoing fine," she wrote, adding that she was more in survival mode financially, professionally, socially and also mentally.Mahajan said she won't say her life in the UK was a failure, but it made her able to go back to India. "I got to travel more than I ever imagined, meet people from all over the world, become much more independent and grow professionally in ways I probably couldnât have anticipated. The UK gave me a lot," she said."For now, being back in India has been good for me. Thereâs still a lot Iâm processing, and Iâm sure Iâll have moments of wondering whether I made the right decision. But Iâm increasingly convinced that not every good decision has to feel euphoric," she said.Reactions to the 'back to India' postSuch 'back to India' social media posts always get some racist comments and there was no exception here too. "I wish you would encourage the other 5 million indians to move back with you. We will definitely not miss you," one wrote."Say you couldn't renew your work visa or your sponsor no longer sponsored you. The sob story is just belittling," another said."Thank god you didnât mention âhaving a maid in Indiaâ as a benefit," a third user wrote.Many Indians, however, supported Mahajan's honesty and said they too went through the same experiencesCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: This rare polyamorous bird of prey’s location has been kept a mystery. Here’s why
articles.summary: The UK’s rarest bird of prey has successfully bred in a secret location for a second consecutive year, with conservationists crediting one polyamorous male with bringing the species back from near extinction in the country.
articles.body: The UK’s rarest bird of prey has successfully bred in a secret location for a second consecutive year, with conservationists crediting one polyamorous male with bringing the species back from near extinction in the country. Montagu’s harriers – raptors referred to as the “aristocrats of the bird world” – were put on a red list of birds most at risk in the UK in 2021, with no breeding pairs spotted between 2020 and 2023. But one adult male known as AU is now keeping Britain’s “Monties” population alive. He’s responsible for at least 16 chicks since 2018, according to the wildlife conservation charity The Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB), including six juveniles that were bred this year with two females in two different nests. AU had previously bred four chicks with a female in 2025, after a six-year wait in the UK for new Montagu’s harrier families. “When we ringed him as a chick in 2016 in a different part of the country we had no idea that ten years later he would single-handedly prop up the species in Britain,” said the RSPB’s Mark Thomas. The charity’s fieldworkers in July fitted one chick from each of the two nests with satellite tracking tags to follow their migration and survival – marking the first time in the UK that juvenile Montagu’s harriers have been tagged. “Monties” travel to Europe from Africa each spring to breed, but only a small number head to the UK, according to the RSPB. AU arrived and began performing his aerial courtship displays in early May, an RSPB spokesperson told CNN. These “acrobatic” displays, known as “skydancing,” feature “high-altitude dives, rhythmic ‘U’-shaped undulations, loops, and twists accompanied by rapid, cackling vocalizations,” the spokesperson said, adding that AU “pulled off the two nests through hard work and a good food supply.” The raptors’ breeding population peaked at around 30 breeding pairs in the mid-1950s, decreasing to zero in 1974, before rising to up to 13 pairs in the late 2000s, according to BTO. A sustained collaboration with farmers and birdwatchers led to breeding success this year and in 2025, said the RSPB, which attributes those gains to keeping the birds’ breeding location under wraps. “This is a sensitive species that is easily disturbed,” the RSPB said, adding that they decided to keep the location of the new nests “a secret” as the birds might also return to the same breeding sites again. Plus, the nests are on private land, they said. One of the two nests spotted this year was found inside a patch of barley left as a habitat by a farmer, with the other nest located less than a mile away, according to the charity.

articles.title: A British metal detectorist thought he'd found a bull's nose ring; it was actually a Bronze Age gold bracelet, and then two more appeared
articles.summary: UK News: In late May, dozens of metal-detecting enthusiasts gathered near Carlisle, in northern England close to the Scottish border, for a rally that also ser.
articles.body: In late May, dozens of metal-detecting enthusiasts gathered near Carlisle, in northern England close to the Scottish border, for a rally that also served as a protest against a proposed electricity substation. Over 4 days, the group searched roughly 470 acres and uncovered hundreds of objects, including a Viking brooch and an 1817 coin bearing the likeness of King George III. Among them was 34-year-old Scottish gas engineer Andy Crammond, who picked up a gleaming gold object he initially mistook for a bull's nose ring. But the object's unusual shine and weight quickly made him suspect it was something much older and more valuable. His friend Alan Daniels came over to inspect the discovery, and the pair soon uncovered 2 more remarkably similar gold objects nearby, revealing an extraordinarily rare Bronze Age find. The discovery transformed an otherwise routine day of searching into an archaeological breakthrough, with specialists later identifying the objects as complete gold torcs dating back more than three millennia. This extraordinary discovery highlights how grassroots archaeological efforts can uncover invaluable historical treasures, potentially reshaping our understanding of ancient civilizations while simultaneously informing crucial modern land-use decisions.Why archaeologists consider 3 complete Bronze Age torcs exceptionally rareAccording to Smithsonian Magazine, the 3 gold objects are torcs dating to around 1100 BCE, placing them around the transition between Britain's Middle and Late Bronze Age. Archaeologist Jim Morris of the University of Lancashire described the discovery as spectacular, noting that surviving torcs from this period are often found as broken fragments rather than complete objects. Morris told BBC News that even finding a single intact torc is unusual, making the discovery of 3 complete examples together particularly significant. The objects have a combined weight of about 18.3 ounces and have been valued at more than $400,000, according to reporting by the Telegraph. The finds have been submitted for assessment under Britain's Treasure Act, which determines whether archaeologically significant discoveries become the property of the Crown and whether finders and landowners may receive a reward.What Bronze Age torcs reveal about wealth, status and ancient communitiesBronze Age torcs could be worn around the neck or wrist, but archaeologists still debate precisely what they represented. Some researchers interpret them as symbols of wealth, status or authority, while others have suggested that particular examples may have had communal, ceremonial or ritual significance. Their physical condition can also provide clues about how they were used. Some surviving torcs show evidence of wear, repair or modification, suggesting that certain objects may have been used for long periods rather than immediately buried.For Crammond and Daniels, however, the discovery was far beyond anything they had previously encountered. Daniels, who has been metal detecting with Crammond as a hobby for several years, told the Telegraph that the pair had never found anything comparable. The remarkable preservation of the objects is partly explained by gold itself. Unlike many metals, gold does not readily corrode or tarnish, allowing the torcs to retain their distinctive appearance after more than 3,000 years underground.How a protest against a power substation led to the Bronze Age discoveryThe discovery has an unusual modern connection: the land where the torcs were found is at the centre of opposition to a proposed electricity project. The site could eventually accommodate infrastructure associated with the Cross Border Connection, a major project intended to strengthen electricity transmission between Scotland and England. Local campaigners have raised concerns about the potential effects of the development on the landscape, wildlife and surrounding communities. Members of Lothian Relics Metal Detecting were invited to search the area as part of efforts to document its archaeological significance before development could take place. Nobody expected the survey to produce 3 complete Bronze Age gold torcs.The discovery has now added another layer to the debate over the site's future. Campaigners say the finds, alongside other archaeological discoveries in the area, demonstrate that the landscape could contain important evidence of Britain's past. For archaeologists, the significance extends beyond the monetary value of the gold. Three complete torcs buried together offer a rare opportunity to investigate Bronze Age craftsmanship, movement, wealth and ritual practices, potentially revealing details about a society that existed more than 3,000 years ago.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: As Ukraine’s allies gather for big anniversary, one key backer is absent
articles.summary: The lack of visible senior Trump administration participation was the latest sign of how Washington has backed off during a critical juncture for Ukraine.
articles.body: Leaders of Ukraine’s international allies on Monday marked 35 years since the country broke away from the Soviet Union to become an independent nation. The U.K.’s Andy Burnham flew in, while France’s Emmanuel Macron and Germany’s Friedrich Merz joined a call to reaffirm commitments to Kyiv. But senior officials from one longtime backer were notably absent from the public show of support: the United States. While U.S. senators and former officials visited Ukraine ahead of the commemorations, the apparent lack of senior Trump administration participation was the latest sign of how Washington has backed off during a critical juncture for Ukraine. The message sent was especially pointed as Monday also marks 4 1/2 years since President Vladimir Putin launched his large-scale invasion of Russia’s much smaller neighbor. Negotiations to reach a peace deal, which President Donald Trump once promised to achieve within 24 hours, have stalled as supplies of U.S. air defense missiles dwindle and the Russian leader ramps up threats to Ukraine’s allies. Britain’s Burnham was the highest-profile Western leader to fly in and co-chair a meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing,” a group of countries backing Ukraine. European Council President António Costa, as well as the heads of nearly a dozen European nations, was also in Kyiv, despite the country’s air force reporting Russian rocket and drone strikes overnight. Secretary of State Marco Rubio congratulated Ukraine in a statement. “The United States is committed to Ukraine’s sovereignty and continues to work to support a negotiated settlement to the Russia-Ukraine war that establishes a lasting and durable peace,” it said. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha thanked Rubio for “thoughtful” greetings, adding, “We will be glad to welcome you in Kyiv.” Over the weekend, Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and James Lankford, R-Okla., met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and Blumenthal attended a ceremony Monday. Former Vice President Mike Pence and ex-special envoy for Ukraine Keith Kellogg were also in Kyiv for meetings. Kellogg was considered “too close to Ukraine” by Russian negotiators before he stepped down in December, NBC News reported last year. Late Monday, a State Department spokesperson told NBC News that the newly arrived Chargé d’Affaires, Paul Houston, had attended official commemorations. In response to questions sent to the White House about the lack of senior administration representation at the events, a U.S. official said: “President Trump’s representatives speak with Ukrainian officials almost daily, and the United States has done more than anyone to bring this bitter war to an end.” On Tuesday, Zelenskyy said he received “warm and heartening congratulations” from Trump. The U.S. was once Ukraine’s most important supporter, providing billions of dollars in military aid and sharing critical intelligence. But since Trump returned to the Oval Office in early 2025, significant new aid has ceased, with the U.S. selling weapons to Ukraine’s NATO partners to be transferred to Kyiv instead. An analysis of how American aid flows have changed by the Council on Foreign Relations, a nonpartisan U.S. think tank, showed that as of March this year, Congress has made available $195 billion in spending related to the war in Ukraine. Of the $195 billion, $164 billion came from five pieces of legislation, the last of which was passed in April 2024, according to the report. U.K. and French support In recent days, the U.K. and France announced they would share critical military technology to help Ukraine defend itself. Britain has agreed to allow European missile manufacturer MBDA to release classified information on British-made components used in the SCALP long-range cruise missile. With the information from the U.K., Ukraine will be able to establish local assembly lines to produce the missile, which shares British and French technology, according to Downing Street. Zelenskyy also said this weekend that France’s Macron has agreed to accelerate the delivery of the latest French equipment and missiles. The European Commission also approved a further $7.1 billion in financial aid for Ukraine on Monday to procure new defense systems, such as air defense, missiles, ammunition and radars. With Moscow firing larger volleys of high-speed rockets at Ukraine’s cities, the country is staring down a long and perilous winter as it runs out of critically important interceptors capable of taking down Russian ballistic missiles. Zelenskyy has pleaded with the U.S., the main maker of the interceptors for the Patriot missile air defense systems, to send Kyiv more, but the Iran war has depleted supplies and left Washington rationing remaining stock. A severe shortage of interceptors combined with a harsh winter and Russian strikes on Ukraine’s energy grid could force Kyiv to come to the negotiating table under unfavorable terms. This is not the message that Zelenskyy sought to transmit, however. “Ukraine absolutely wants peace, but it is not ready to simply surrender,” he said in a defiant speech Monday.

articles.title: The latest dangerous social media trend that ‘gamifies’ deadly driving
articles.summary: The long month of August is typically one of the busiest times of the year for police, with schools out for summer and many young people at a loose end.
articles.body: The long month of August is typically one of the busiest times of the year for police, with schools out for summer and many young people at a loose end. From the so-called “teen takeovers” sparking curfews across the United States, to the “blackout challenge” where users choke themselves, viral and occasionally dangerous challenges spurred on by social media have become a draw for some youngsters. This summer though across Britain and Ireland, a new, dangerous trend has emerged. One which involves groups of mostly young men filming what have been dubbed “wrong-way” driving videos, and then posting them online. The British government called on social media companies to remove videos which celebrate dangerous driving on Monday, after a string of deadly crashes in the UK and Ireland involving people driving cars the wrong way down major roads. As a result, tech companies have come under the spotlight amid reports of viral footage circulating online depicting risky driving, with local officials warning that “likes” on social media are being prioritised over the safety of innocent people. Authorities are probing the exact causes of the latest crashes. One incident over the weekend saw two police officers and five young people killed near Middlesbrough, northern England after a vehicle traveling on the wrong side of the street collided with a marked police car. The five occupants of the car, a Volkswagen Passat, were between the ages of 17 and 23, police said. A now-deleted TikTok account believed to belong to one of the teenagers who died in the crash includes a video, posted in March 2025, of him and four other young people involved in what appears to be a police car chase, according to the BBC. Another video shared by the same profile appears to show a speedometer with a reading of 100mph (160kph), the BBC said. There were swift tributes to the courage of the two police officers who were killed, named as Matthew Blades, aged 37, and Tom Clough, aged 38. Police said later Monday they had arrested 12 people as part of a probe into criminal activity which occurred prior to the crash. Several reports were received about two vehicles being driven dangerously, including one which was said to be “ramming properties,” police said. Warning to tech companies On Monday, British Defence Minister Luke Pollard called on social media firms to remove content which shows risky driving, including cars traveling “down the wrong side of the roads.” “There’s lots of content online on social media platforms of people celebrating dangerous driving, celebrating driving inappropriately on our roads, down the wrong side of the roads, behaving incredibly badly,” Pollard told the BBC. “We’ve already spoken to those companies as a government, telling them that we’ll use the powers in the Online Safety Act” to ensure dangerous content is taken down, Pollard said, referring to legislation in the UK which mandates tech companies to protect users from illegal and harmful content. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham later said people who share footage glorifying dangerous driving are “doing something that’s truly reprehensible.” In response to the latest crash, social media giant TikTok said it was closely monitoring any online content related to the incident and is removing videos and accounts that break the company’s rules. The website of Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, says content which promotes “high-risk viral challenges” is removed, while imagery depicting reckless driving that could lead to life-threatening injuries or death is restricted for under 18s, “except if shared in fictional or professional settings.” ‘Irresponsible and dangerous’ The incident near Middlesbrough is not isolated, with local officials discussing the dangers of the social media trend in the context of several other deadly car crashes. Earlier in August, five teenagers were killed in a two-vehicle collision in Ireland after driving a car the wrong way down a motorway. Three women and a boy, who were in the second vehicle, were hospitalized with serious injuries. The head of Irish police, Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly, said the incident showed how “irresponsible and dangerous driving on the wrong side of the motorway is,” while saying his thoughts were with those injured. “What makes this reckless behaviour even more appalling is that in some cases it is being done for social media likes regardless of the potentially devastating impact it might have on innocent people and themselves,” Kelly said at the time. Also, earlier this month, Irish police made an appeal for witnesses after a car carrying eight boys collided head-on with another vehicle while travelling northbound on the southbound carriageway of a motorway near Dublin, resulting in serious injury. The true extent of the social media trend remains unclear, but Irish broadcaster RTÉ said Monday that 62 incidents of people driving the wrong way down motorways have been recorded so far this year in Ireland, citing the body which oversees Ireland’s roads and public transport networks, 32% more than in the same period last year. Reckless driving is not a new behavior, but it can now be “recorded and broadcast to millions for views, for likes, and for followers. So, the danger becomes the content,” said Mary Aiken, a professor of cyberpsychology from Capital Technology University in Washington, DC. Aiken told CNN she believes the act of recording the risky driving creates a “perceived distance from real-world danger” for the driver. “I believe that what they’re doing starts to feel like a game or a live performance, and the likes, the views and the follower counts provide visible and immediate social rewards,” she said. She said it should be “extremely straightforward” for social media companies to take down content which glorifies this “criminal and high-risk behavior.” TikTok said it removes content which glorifies violence or promotes crimes using a range of techniques, including human moderation, detection technologies and user reporting. Between January and March of this year, the company said that of the content it removed for violating its policies on violent and criminal behavior, 99.1% was taken down before it was reported to them. ‘An adored son and brother’ While Matt Storey, the police commissioner for Cleveland where the Middlesbrough crash occurred, said it was too early to comment on the cause of the collision, he stated that any filming while driving was “absolutely ridiculous” and “idiotic.” “It is a worrying situation if that’s becoming more prevalent because it is incredibly dangerous,” he told BBC Radio 4. Pollard added that he wanted to see the outcome of the police investigation before he can “understand what precisely happened in the tragedy here.” In tributes to the officers killed, released by police, Clough’s family said he was a “hero” who was “willing to help anyone for any reason,” while Blades’ wife described him as “an adored son and brother, a perfect son-in-law and the most fun uncle.”

articles.title: 12 people arrested in connection with UK A66 crash that killed 7, including 2 police officers
articles.summary: UK News: Twelve individuals have been arrested in connection with a tragic accident on the A66 in the UK that resulted in the deaths of seven people, including two police officers. Investigations into organized crime and vehicle involvement are ongoing.
articles.body: Twelve people have been arrested in connection with criminal activity allegedly linked to a crash on the UK's A66 that killed seven people, including two police officers.Cleveland Police said nine men and three women, aged between 19 and 61, were detained as part of a wider investigation into the circumstances surrounding the fatal collision near Middlesbrough.The crash happened when a Volkswagen Passat travelling in the wrong direction on the A66 collided with a marked armed response vehicle carrying PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough. Both officers died in the collision.Five men travelling in the Passat also died. They were aged between 17 and 23 and were pronounced dead at the scene.Police said those arrested are suspected of offences ranging from firearm possession to involvement in an organised crime group. Four of the five men who died in the Passat had previously been convicted of offences, according to investigators.Investigation into criminal activityThe arrests form part of what Cleveland Police described as a large-scale investigation into criminal activity connected to the fatal collision.Officers from Durham, Northumbria and North Yorkshire police forces have assisted with the investigation.Police have also recovered a Volvo XC60 which investigators believe was connected to the activities of people travelling in the Passat.Assistant Chief Constable Wayne Fox said the investigation had involved serious and organised crime and would continue.He said: âWe have a duty to respond to, and thoroughly investigate, the serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident, and to bring all those responsible to justice.âFox also paid tribute to the two officers who died and said colleagues had continued working despite the impact of their deaths.He added that the incident would have a lasting effect on the Cleveland community and thanked members of the public and police forces for their support.Cleveland Police has also addressed reports of an increase in videos showing dangerous driving being shared online.The force said there was âno evidence to indicate that filming of the activities that took place on Friday night and Saturday morning has taken place for TikTokâCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Israeli strikes hit water plant, warehouse in Gaza, killing at least seven
articles.summary: Two Palestinian children among victims as Israeli attacks on Gaza continue despite US-brokered ceasefire.
articles.body:
Israeli forces have launched attacks across Gaza, hitting a mosque, a water desalination plant and tents housing displaced people, killing at least seven people and wounding several others.

The victims on Monday included at least two children , including a four-year-old boy, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.

In central Gaza, an Israeli strike hit a house in the Bureij refugee camp, killing a child, identified as four-year-old Hassan al-Hafi, according to Wafa.

In southern Gaza, another child, identified as Amal Nash’at Abu Khater, died from gunshot wounds after Israeli forces fired on her in Khan Younis.

Another man died of wounds sustained during an Israeli raid on a tent in central Deir el-Balah early on Monday, Wafa reported, adding that two others also died from injuries sustained during Israeli attacks last week.

The deaths came a day after Israeli forces killed three Palestinians, including another four-year-old child, in attacks on Khan Younis and the town of az-Zawayda.

The ongoing strikes come despite a United States-brokered ceasefire to end Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and amid diplomatic efforts to disarm Hamas and get Israeli troops to withdraw from the Gaza Strip.

Al Jazeera’s Tareq Abu Azzoum, reporting from Deir el-Balah, said the Israeli military issued forced displacement orders for at least four sites in Gaza ahead of Monday’s attacks.

They included strikes on a water desalination plant, a mosque and a warehouse holding humanitarian supplies.

“These sites are considered safe under the ceasefire agreement, but the Israeli military has been intensifying attacks under the pretext of security,” Abu Azzoum said. “People on the ground say the ceasefire has effectively represented an extension of the war itself, as attacks continue without respite. Many remain sceptical about the next phase of Israeli military action – whether the security pretext will be used to justify further operations here in Gaza.”

A total of 1,288 Palestinians have been killed since the October 2025 ceasefire agreement, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry.

The total death toll since the genocidal war on Gaza was launched in October 2023 has risen to 73,422, with a further 174,401 wounded.

articles.title: Network Rail sues companies for £5m over Llanegennech derailment
articles.summary: More than 400,000 litres of fuel spilled in the area causing an "environmental disaster".
articles.body:
Network Rail is suing two rail companies for more than £5m after a fuel spill caused by a train derailment threatened an "environmental disaster" at a designated site for protection.

The body filed a legal claim earlier this month against DB Cargo UK and Touax Rail over the derailment near Llangennech, Carmarthenshire, in August 2020.

The incident saw 10 wagons of the 25-wagon train derail , causing 446,000 litres of fuel to spill, and about 300 people had to leave the area due to the blaze.

In High Court documents, Network Rail claimed that the derailment occurred because the wagon had "not been maintained with reasonable care" and is seeking damages for negligence.

No one was injured, but 116,000 litres of fuel ignited while 330,000 litres drained into surrounding wetlands, which form part of a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) and a Special Area of Conservation.

The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) concluded in January 2022 that the derailment was caused by a set of wheels on one of the wagons locking, likely the result of a brake defect after "inadequate maintenance practices" were found in the investigation.

Network Rail, which owns, operates, maintains and develops Britain's railways, claimed that the derailment occurred because the wagon had "not been maintained with reasonable care" by Touax.

It is also seeking damages from DB Cargo UK, claiming that the latter "breached a contractual duty to ensure that reasonable care was taken" in maintaining the wagon.

Lawyers for the body said it expected to recover "more than £5m" with DB Cargo and Touax yet to file defences.

A hearing in the case is due to take place.

The locomotive was pulling the wagons from Milford Haven, Pembrokeshire, to Theale, near Reading, when the derailment occurred.

The line was closed for six months after the incident and did not fully reopen for almost a year, with 30,000 tonnes of fuel-soaked soil having to be excavated.

Bill Kelly, the then-Network Rail Wales route director, said when the line fully reopened in March 2021 that work following the incident was "one of the biggest environmental recovery operations Network Rail has ever been involved with".

He added that the derailment could have caused a "total environmental disaster".

The RAIB said, in its 2022 report, that the train was travelling at about 38mph at the time of the derailment, and was carrying up to 75.5 tonnes of fuel.

The RAIB did not establish blame or liability for the incident, but made nine recommendations to avoid similar accidents.

Network Rail and DB Cargo declined to comment, while Touax has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Japan lawmakers visit China seeking to ease tensions over Taiwan
articles.summary: A cross-party delegation lands in Beijing as Tokyo tries to defrost its worst China rift in decades.
articles.body:
Japanese lawmakers have travelled to Beijing in a bid to soothe strained relations between the two nations.

The delegation landed in China on Monday for talks aimed at restoring communication. The mission was undertaken after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi issued comments on Taiwan that triggered a diplomatic dispute that has begun to weigh on economic relations.

list 3 of 3 US accuses dozens of countries of helping China avoid Trump’s tariffs

The visit will run through Thursday and marks the first such consultations with senior Chinese Communist Party officials since ties soured late last year.

Relations plunged after Takaichi suggested in November that Japan could respond militarily if China attacked Taiwan, a self-governing island that Beijing claims as its own territory.

China is highly sensitive regarding Taiwan and considers questioning of its claim on the island a red line. In response to Takaichi’s comments, it warned its citizens against travel to Japan and tightened trade restrictions, including measures that reportedly disrupted the flow of rare earth minerals to Japanese firms, adding an economic sting to the diplomatic fallout.

Among those making the trip was Gaku Hashimoto, a member of the House of Representatives and Takaichi’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party. He was joined by other lawmakers from the opposition Komeito and Centrist Reform Alliance parties.

An official from Hashimoto’s office confirmed only that he had “departed for Beijing to stay for two days”.

Before leaving Tokyo, delegation member Shinichi Isa, a spokesperson for the Centrist Reform Alliance, told reporters: “Communication has been severed in all areas, and we are beginning to see their impact in many areas. I hope we can somehow find a clue to restart a dialogue.”

Isa, a former diplomat at the Japanese embassy in China, had already sounded the alarm over the situation this month in a post on X, writing that officials had always managed to stay in contact even during past low points but now “all channels between officials and ministries have been cut off.”

He described the current state of relations as the worst since diplomatic ties were normalised in 1972.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Friday that “some people of insight from both Japan’s ruling and opposition parties” were troubled by the state of relations and hoped to help steer them back on track while calling on Tokyo to heed those voices and act to restore normal exchanges between the two countries.

Takaichi has not retracted her comment on Taiwan and is yet to respond to the concerns.

Further exchanges are planned. Former Japanese Foreign Minister Takeshi Iwaya is expected to lead another delegation to China in late September, which is to be followed by a group of Japanese business representatives later in the year, according to the Kyodo News agency.

articles.title: Outrage in Nepal over rape and murder of three-year-old girl
articles.summary: There have been protests since the girl was found dead last week, three days after she went missing.
articles.body:
Activists and politicians in Nepal have urged the government to enact tougher laws as the alleged rape and murder of a three-year-old girl has caused outrage across the country.

Nepal has seen continued protests since the girl was found dead last week, three days after she went missing in Madhesh province.

Nine people have been arrested in connection with the case, a local police spokesman told the BBC.

The crime has triggered demands for reform. Police have also been accused of negligence in the initial stages of the investigation after footage of a teenage suspect was leaked onto social media.

After days of demonstrations in the city of Simara, the victim's family met government ministers, and secured a written agreement over the weekend.

The government has promised to review laws on serious offences, and create a memorial in honour of the child.

The incident has also opened a wider debate over how Nepal deals with young offenders, with some campaigners pushing for harsher punishments for minors convicted of rape or murder.

Prominent human rights activist Gauri Pradhan called the attack a "very painful incident and the government should punish anyone involved in such atrocious act. There should be some serious efforts for wider reforms".

However, he cautioned against calls for the introduction of the death penalty.

There has also been anger after a video showing a teenage suspect giving a statement about the suspected murder was uploaded to social media, sparking questions as to how footage of the individual under police custody was leaked.

"We have so far found one police personnel directly involved in the [leak] and have initiated action against him," chief district officer of Bara district, Dharmendra Kumar Mishra, told the BBC.

"If more officers are found, they will also be punished. We have zero tolerance against such practice."

More than 25,500 accusations of rape and sexual abuse were filed between July 2017 to July 2025, according to Nepalese Police.

Of these cases, more than 3,200 female victims were under the age of 10, the police say.

articles.title: Canada’s opposition leader demands Carney reconvene Parliament after US trade talks collapse
articles.summary: Canadian opposition leader Pierre Poilievre pressed his country’s prime minister, Mark Carney, to reconvene the Canadian Parliament amid trade tensions with the U.S. “As Canadians are vulnerable to an escalating trade war with the United States, Parliament must be reconvened. Canadians deserve answers on how trade talks collapsed, what tariffs will cost their families, and…
articles.body:
Canadian opposition leader Pierre Poilievre pressed his country’s prime minister, Mark Carney, to reconvene the Canadian Parliament amid trade tensions with the U.S.

“As Canadians are vulnerable to an escalating trade war with the United States, Parliament must be reconvened. Canadians deserve answers on how trade talks collapsed, what tariffs will cost their families, and how their jobs will be protected,” Poilievre, the leader of Canada’s Conservative Party in the Canadian Parliament, said Monday in a post on the social platform X .

“Prime Minister, reconvene Parliament now,” he added.

Poilievre’s post also featured a letter to Carney in which the opposition leader said that “the failure to secure a durable trade agreement, together with escalating tariffs, now threatens deeper economic pain on top of a decade of rising costs and zero economic growth in the Canadian economy.”

Carney removed Canadian negotiators from trade discussions with the U.S. on Friday, shortly before a fresh round of tariffs from the Trump administration went into effect. He said a day later that his country would implement retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. starting on Sept. 8, responding to the new 50 percent tariffs from the Trump administration.

During a press conference, Carney said Canada would “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses.”

Throughout President Trump’s second term, tensions have erupted between the U.S. and Canada, two countries that have historically shared a strong alliance, over tariff policy. The president has also pushed for Canada to become the U.S.’s 51st state, to Canadian opposition.

The Hill has reached out to Carney’s office for comment.

Kidnappers have released a video of what appears to be a large group of people being held captive by armed men in a forested area in Nigeria.

The video emerged on Sunday, two days after gunmen abducted as many as 600 worshippers during Friday prayers at a mosque in Dekera village in Nigeria’s north-central Niger state.

articles.title: 9 commons myths about wrinkles debunked — and what dermatologists want you to know instead
articles.summary: From the importance of genetics to whether $200 moisturizers are a good buy, here's the whole truth and nothing but the truth.
articles.body:
Our experts independently review everything we recommend. If you buy through our links, we may earn commission.

I once read about a lady who didn't smile for over 40 years . Her reason for such a stationary expression was not a distaste for joy and laughter, but something else entirely — to prevent wrinkles . She'd decided that maintaining a straight, expressionless face was worth it to keep smooth, youthful-looking skin. (Apparently, she even resisted smiling when her daughter was born! Can you imagine?)

Sometimes, when I'm slathering on my lotions and potions in the evening, I think about this woman. Not because it's a cautionary tale about vanity, but because her fear wasn't necessarily directed at the right thing. Wrinkle mythology is full of misplaced fears and misplaced faith. We treat certain habits like miracle workers and others like poison, often with evidence pointed in the opposite direction. So, instead of guessing what to do and what to avoid, I asked dermatologists to bust some wrinkle myths and misconceptions. (But as the great Oscar Wilde once said, "The truth is rarely pure and never simple.")

Myth #1: Facial expressions are the main cause of wrinkles

Let's address the aforementioned smile-averse situation. If we stop facial movement, whether it's a smile, frown or Elvis-like lip snarl, it would stop wrinkles, right? According to Dr. Behrooz Torkian , a double board-certified facial plastic surgeon based in Beverly Hills, Calif., it's not that simple. Now, some wrinkles really are caused by movement: "A prime example of this is the wrinkles on the forehead, the glabella, or so-called 'elevens,' and the crow's feet," he says. But movement is also competing with bigger forces like sun exposure and collagen loss. His advice is to limit repetitive movement with Botox where it matters, and protect collagen with adequate SPF , a good diet, stress control and no smoking.

To rebuild collagen, Torkian recommends vitamin C , retinoids , growth factors and peptides , along with regular microneedling, radio frequency and laser treatments. And if you happen to have a red light mask in your closet, now's the time to break it out. "Recent scientific evidence on red light therapy has also supported the use of red and near-infrared light to support the metabolic processes of building collagen in the skin," he says.

Myth #2: How much you wrinkle depends solely on genetics

Your bloodline may set things up for your skin, but it doesn't decide the outcome alone. "Genetics matter because your genes shape how thick your skin is, how well you hold onto collagen and how much melanin you have doing built-in sun protection," says Dr. Geeta Yadav, a board-certified dermatologist and founder of Facet Dermatology. This is part of why some people "start creasing in their 30s while others sail into their 60s looking smooth."

However, she points out how identical twins with identical DNA can look years apart in age. She underscores the sun's impact on our skin, which makes movement seem like a minor threat by comparison. "Sun alone is estimated to account for around 80% of the visible aging we see on the face," she says.

Myth #3: The more expensive the moisturizer, the better

By now, you probably know that drugstore beauty can go toe-to-toe with luxury brands , and moisture is no exception. "I have always believed that paying a lot for a moisturizer is not worth it," says Torkian. What matters, he says, is what's actually in the jar. Moisturizers break down into three parts: humectants that draw in water, emollients that soften and occlusives that seal it all in. Beyond that, you want to consider whether it has actives, such as peptides, retinoids, hydroxy acids and niacinamide. "As a general rule, I personally avoid the super expensive and the super cheap," he says.

Myth #4: Dry skin causes wrinkles; oily skin ages better

"One of the most essential factors in the appearance of wrinkles in skin is the hydration of the collagen, hyaluronic acid and elastin within the dermis and epidermis," explains Torkian. Oil definitely supports it, as more sebaceous glands mean the skin has a built-in defense system against losing that moisture. However, dry skin doesn't necessarily mean you're doomed. It just needs that same protection in a different way: "Moisturizers such as ceramides to augment the skin barrier" versus retinoids and hydroxy acids for oily skin — at least as a starting point.

According to Torkian, internal hydration is definitely a part of the picture, but only if the skin barrier is already intact and topical moisture is in place. But water alone doesn't do the plumping. A 2015 study published in Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology showed that adding roughly 2 liters of water a day to women's diets for a month significantly improved skin hydration and biomechanics.

Ultimately, it's less that water plumps wrinkles and more that dehydration accelerates them. Yadav is more blunt, saying that drinking more water is unlikely to meaningfully change wrinkles.

Myth #6: Retinol and tretinoin are interchangeable

Both retinol and tretinoin speed up cell turnover and rebuild collagen, which smooths and softens wrinkles over time. But the real question is which one gets you there and how fast. Torkian breaks down how tretinoin is the active compound itself, whereas retinol has to go through two steps to convert into tretinoin. "This means that using tretinoin can lead to quicker results and quicker onset of the results, but it can also feel a little bit more harsh to skin that has not adjusted to retinoic acid yet," he says. Over the long term, results from both can be very similar, he adds.

Myth #7: Only in-office procedures can reverse wrinkles, not topicals

According to Torkian, the answer to this isn't a flat no. "There are some topicals that can be very helpful in reversing wrinkling," he says, "provided that the wrinkling has not gone out of hand." Retinoids, especially prescription tretinoin, have decades of trial evidence behind them, while vitamin C, growth factors and peptides can also make a difference.

But he doesn't stop there: "Another essential factor is whether proper prevention is being employed at the same time as using the topical that is intended to reverse wrinkling." In other words, a product working solo, without sun protection or consistency, applied to wrinkles that are already deeply set isn't a fair test of what topicals can actually do.

Myth #8: The neck and chest age faster than the face

While it's true that the skin on the neck and chest is very different from the skin on the face (mainly because there are fewer oil glands), Torkian pushes back on the framing of this myth, and points out the impact of our behavior. "One thing to keep in mind about the skin of the neck and chest is that they rarely get any love," he says. "I always like to remind my patients that when they have their skin-care routine, they should not forget the neck and chest. It is natural to want to use all of your expensive skin-care products on what you feel people are looking at the most, but spreading a little love below the chin can be impactful over time in preventing neck and chest aging."

Myth #9: Botox is the best treatment for all kinds of wrinkles

Yadav is clear that Botox is excellent for softening the dynamic lines caused by repeated muscle movement. "Frown lines, forehead lines and crow's feet respond beautifully, because quieting the muscle stops it folding the skin above it thousands of times a day," she explains. But it does much less for lines already etched in when your face is completely at rest, and very little for crepey texture, sun damage or the sagging that comes from lost volume and laxity, she says.

At under $10, this effective cream is proof of Myth #3 — you don't have to splurge to get real results. It pairs retinol with bakuchiol, a plant-derived retinol alternative that helps soften irritation, plus vitamin E and allantoin to keep skin calm. You get softer-looking lines and plumper, less flakey skin without the retinol redness.

One of the most effective anti-aging treatments available without a prescription is Differin. This dermatologist favorite can help improve skin texture, fine lines and overall skin tone as long as you're consistent. It can also help build collagen, which, in turn, makes skin look brighter and bouncier.

This budget-friendly moisturizer does barrier-repair work while you sleep thanks to a powerful trio of ceramides, hyaluronic acid and peptides. It's essentially the ingredient-category cheat sheet from Myth #6 packed into an affordable cream.

We voted this the best drugstore face serum for a reason. It contains Vichy's legendary Volcanic Water, which is sourced from French volcanoes and contains 15 essential minerals that strengthen, protect and repair the skin barrier​.

This Celimax cream features a two-in-one dispenser, releasing a retinal cream with 5% panthenol soothing cream at the same time. It also explicitly treats the neck alongside the face with matrixyl 3000, a peptide complex, for firming, so you can make sure Myth #8 gets covered.

articles.title: A West Sussex widow transformed £57,000 fly-tipped wasteland into a dream mini-farm with pigs, chickens and 2,000 plants; now she has been ordered to tear it down after losing a planning battle
articles.summary: UK News: When Tara Dexter bought a neglected patch of land in Sidlesham, West Sussex, for £57,000, it was far from the countryside dream she had imagined. The .
articles.body: When Tara Dexter bought a neglected patch of land in Sidlesham, West Sussex, for £57,000, it was far from the countryside dream she had imagined. The site was reportedly filled with rubbish, car parts and other dumped waste. But for Dexter, 57, the property represented something much bigger. It was an opportunity to fulfil a dream she had once shared with her late partner, Gary, while also giving herself a place to heal after his death from cancer.Today, the site has been transformed into a smallholding filled with plants, pigs, chickens, peacocks and wildlife. But Dexter has now been given just four months to dismantle key parts of the project after her planning appeal was rejected.From fly-tipped wasteland to thriving smallholdingAccording to the Daily Mail, Dexter said she spent years clearing rubbish and transforming the land into what she describes as her dream micro-farm.The property now has around 2,000 plants, raised beds, fencing and hedgerows. Deer and buzzards visit the site, while Dexter also keeps pigs, chickens and peacocks.She created a willow igloo that is used by disabled children who visit the site, while pupils from a nearby primary school have also taken part in outdoor activities there.But the very structures Dexter says are essential to running the smallholding have become the centre of a planning dispute.‘This project has literally saved my life’For Dexter, the mini-farm is not simply a business or hobby. She says it helped her cope with the devastating loss of Gary.Her partner, a former Army veteran, was diagnosed with Stage 4 brain cancer at the age of 52 after suffering a seizure at work. He died just six weeks later.“He was my soulmate,” Dexter told the publication, recalling their relationship. “This project has literally saved my life.”The couple had first met when Dexter was 17 and Gary was 18 before reconnecting later in life. They had dreamed of owning a piece of countryside where they could create a smallholding inspired by the 1970s sitcom The Good Life.After Gary’s death, Dexter decided to pursue that dream on her own.“I worked all the hours I could transforming it and clearing the rubbish and mess from the site,” she said. “It now has around 2,000 plants, fencing, hedgerows and has been cleared of all the toxic rubbish that was here.”£20,000 container becomes centre of planning disputeAs part of the transformation, Dexter purchased a container for £20,000 and clad it with wood so that it would blend into the surrounding landscape.She claims that when she initially discussed the container with the council, she was told there would be no issue with it provided it was raised from the ground or placed on bricks.However, when she later applied for retrospective planning permission, the application was rejected and an enforcement notice was issued.Dexter says the situation became even more frustrating because Chichester District Council had previously awarded her almost £3,000 in grants to plant hedgerows, trees and plants on the land.“It seems like one department doesn't talk to the other. I was getting conflicting messages,” she said.Council says the site is in a floodplainChichester District Council said the planning application for the container was refused in 2024 because it conflicted with policies designed to protect the countryside and because the site is located within a floodplain.The council maintained that the planning decision was based on established policies governing development in the area.The Planning Inspectorate subsequently dismissed Dexter’s appeal.The Inspector found that the container was harmful to the rural setting and was “uncharacteristic” of the area. While acknowledging that there could be a functional need for welfare facilities, secure storage and facilities for educational visits, the Inspector concluded that Dexter had not demonstrated that the same benefits could not be achieved in a less harmful way.‘It seems they would rather have a fly-tipped wasteland’Dexter has strongly criticised the decision and said she believes the council would rather see the land return to its former condition.“It's absolutely ridiculous. It seems the council and planners would rather have a fly-tipped wasteland than a managed smallholding,” she said.“The place was an absolute tip when I took it over and I have totally transformed it and spent huge amounts of time, money and effort to make sure it blends with the environment and contributes to the wildlife.”She also pointed to other nearby plots, claiming they include a burnt-out barn and significant amounts of fly-tipping that she says have gone unaddressed.Dexter said the visits from schoolchildren and the wildlife attracted to the site made the decision particularly painful.“Schoolchildren come on visits and are amazed by the rich variety of wildlife, flowers and plants. It's such a shame,” she said.Widow fears losing the place that helped her healDexter now says she cannot continue operating the mini-farm without the container and sheds and may ultimately be forced to sell the land.“My mental health has not been great since Gary passed away,” she said. “My micro-farm has been my retreat for the past two and half years and I don't know what I'm going to do without it.”The Planning Inspectorate has given Dexter four months to comply with the enforcement requirements.She must remove the metal container building, dismantle and remove two timber buildings, break up and remove four timber planters and remove the concrete hardstanding and concrete plinths, along with all resulting debris.For Dexter, the dispute is about far more than buildings and planning regulations. The smallholding represents a dream she once shared with her partner and the place where she found a reason to keep moving forward after his death.“I am devastated this will all stop,” she said. “I hope the council and planners enjoy it when this place returns to a foul, toxic scrap of wasteland for fly-tippers.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Bessent warns Iran’s global partners to cut ties or face ‘Operation Economic Outcast’
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday issued a global warning for countries to cut any financial ties with Iran or risk being cut off from the U.S. dollar system, launching a new economic pressure campaign against the Islamic Republic as the military front has reached a stalemate six months into the war. Called “Operation Economic…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday issued a global warning for countries to cut any financial ties with Iran or risk being cut off from the U.S. dollar system, launching a new economic pressure campaign against the Islamic Republic as the military front has reached a stalemate six months into the war.

Called “Operation Economic Outcast,” the campaign is marketed as a financial “D-Day” akin to the American invasion of Normandy in World War II. But Bessent’s highly anticipated remarks offered few specific, public actions and instead appeared to serve as a stern advisory.

“Well, we are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior, why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent responded to a question on the lack of specifics or immediate action.

He said President Trump is making calls to world leaders and that officials from the Defense, Treasury and State departments are calling counterparts demanding action in severing ties with Tehran.

Bessent held back naming and shaming specific governments or publicizing timelines for action but said they are being communicated behind the scenes.

“We’re not going to name names. We’ve already seen some results, and I am confident the president, as you all know, is quite persuasive,” Bessent said at a press conference announcing the sanctions plan.

“I would expect that very quickly, if they do not respond, then you will see the ramifications of their actions.”

Absent from Bessent’s remarks was whether the administration will take specific action against China, Iran’s largest trading partner and primary destination for its oil exports — although these have declined sharply over the course of the war. Trump is scheduled to welcome Chinese President Xi Jinping for a state visit on Sept. 24, where the two want to advance a trade deal.

Bessent said no country “is above the reach of U.S. sanctions,” when asked if the administration was pulling punches on Beijing.

“We find that the best way to engage with countries is through quiet diplomacy, and we are level-setting with every country to tell them our expectations,” he said.

The administration has earlier sanctioned Chinese entities processing Iranian oil.

Alongside the announcement, the Treasury Department outlined that it was expanding its authority to sanction any person, regardless of location, for operating in specific sectors of the Iranian economy. These include digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. It further announced new sanctions against 60 entities, individuals and vessels related to Iran’s nuclear and missile technology programs, its ability to conduct cyber operations and generate oil revenue.

“Treasury has mapped every node, every facilitator, and every network that Iran has used to smuggle oil and evade sanctions,” Bessent said.

He called for international branches of Iran’s Bank Melli closed and further teased that a major announcement of sanctions against a financial institution would take place by the end of the week.

The secretary projected the choice before Iran as “complete global isolation and a subsistence economy, or a path back to normalcy with an opportunity to rejoin the global economy.”

Trump has said his aim of going to war with Iran at the end of February was to prevent the country from ever building a nuclear weapon. But Iran has withstood six months of U.S. military attacks — initially in coordination with Israel — demonstrated its ability to hold the Strait of Hormuz hostage and walked away from diplomatic talks with the U.S. over its nuclear program.

The U.S. has responded by imposing a naval blockade against Iran in the strait, which has severely diminished the amount of Iranian oil exported by sea.

Iran’s currency, the rial, reached a record low Monday, declining to approximately 2.02 million to the U.S. dollar. Trump, in a post on his social media site Truth Social, said Iran is “in Economic and Military Death Spiral.” In a separate post he said “IRAN IS COMPLETELY COLLAPSING!!!”

But Iran’s ability to militarily threaten ships in the Strait of Hormuz has created an effective chokehold on the key maritime waterway, raising energy prices globally and stifling Persian Gulf energy exports. A U.S. campaign to escort ships out of the strait has failed to restore transit to prewar levels.

Gas prices in the U.S. again reached over $4 per gallon in the last month, according to AAA.

Iran’s Parliament speaker who earlier negotiated with the U.S., Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, pushed back on the U.S. economic pressure campaign in a statement posted to the social platform X.

“Americans know that no one buys their bombast; the United States is not in an economic position to further restrict its relations with other countries,” he wrote .

“Iran’s trading partners, both in the media and through messages sent to us, have made it clear that they don’t take these statements into account anywhere.”

Still, while the United Arab Emirates attempted a rapprochement with Iran, Abu Dhabi announced last week it was cutting trade ties with Tehran after coming under renewed military attacks.

articles.title: Prince Harry quits African conservation charity after rangers’ human rights abuses
articles.summary: African Parks was embroiled in scandal after it admitted that some of its rangers committed human rights violations.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Prince Harry has resigned from another African charity , marking his second exit from an Africa-focused charity in over a year.

The Duke of Sussex has resigned from the board of wildlife charity African Parks ahead of his move back to the United Kingdom, his spokesperson told The Independent .

African Parks was embroiled in scandal last year after it admitted that some of its rangers committed human rights violations.

One allegation accused a guard of beating, raping and torturing Baka people living in Odzala-Kokoua National Park in the Republic of Congo.

Harry’s representative told The Independent that he still supports African Parks.

“The Duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board,” the spokesperson said. “His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks’ mission.”

Harry served six years as president of the conservation organizations and joined its board of directors in 2023.

In May, Survival International, an indigenous rights charity, urged Harry to resign from the African Parks board after he attended a fundraiser for the organization in Scottsdale, Ariz., drawing criticism from the group.

“It is outrageous to see Harry’s continued support to African Parks despite the horrific human rights abuses committed by its rangers against the Baka,” Survival International Director Caroline Pearce told the British newspaper The Times .

In March 2025, Harry stepped down from Sentebale, the charity he co-founded in Lesotho, Africa, in what he called a breakdown in leadership.

The charity’s chair, Dr. Sophie Chandauka, accused the charity of fostering an environment rife with abuse, including accusing Harry of coordinating a campaign of bullying and harassment.

Sentebale sued Harry, as well as another trustee, for defamation.

articles.title: Terror threat looms over coastal destination as US warns attacks could strike without notice

articles.body: Americans are being warned to avoid parts of an African safari destination where terrorists have targeted upscale lodges frequented by international big-game hunters. Mozambique, a southeastern African country across from the island of Madagascar, is the subject of an Aug. 21 updated "Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution" advisory from the U.S. State Department. Officials have also designated multiple areas "Level 4: Do Not Travel" — citing heightened terrorism risks. AMERICANS WARNED POPULAR TRAVEL ROUTES THIS SUMMER COULD CARRY CRIME AND KIDNAPPING RISKS Bordered by Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, Zimbabwe, South Africa and Eswatini, Mozambique is known for its Indian Ocean coastline, beaches and wildlife reserves. Though not a tourist hot spot, Mozambique draws visitors for its safari tourism. It welcomed over 757,400 foreign guests in 2024, according to government statistics. Cabo Delgado Province, a "Do Not Travel" area, is home to safari and wildlife destinations, including Quirimbas National Park. The State Department also warns that terrorist groups in northern Mozambique are "active" and that there is a risk of terrorist violence and attacks. ROBBERIES, ASSAULTS AND RAPES SPUR NEW US TRAVEL WARNING FOR POPULAR CARIBBEAN GETAWAY "Attackers may strike public areas and tourist destinations with little or no warning, sometimes taking hostages," the advisory says. Alex Perry, an England-based author and veteran foreign correspondent who previously served as a TIME bureau chief, told Fox News Digital the terrorist presence in northern Mozambique is relatively small but particularly brutal. "Mozambique has one of the smaller ISIS groups in the world," Perry said, estimating it has roughly 500 members. "They are spectacularly nasty." Perry, author of the book "Blood Will Flow" about the deadly Islamist insurgency in Mozambique, said militants in Cabo Delgado have carried out mass beheadings, and that the region's tourism industry has suffered as a result of the insurgency. Cabo Delgado has historically attracted a more exclusive clientele, with smaller numbers of wealthy visitors paying high prices for hunting safaris compared with Africa's major mass-market safari destinations, he also said. "They are spectacularly nasty." "This is almost exclusively hunting safaris — people going to shoot animals," Perry said. "That tends to be much smaller numbers of people paying a much higher price." The State Department says Americans who opt to travel to Mozambique are encouraged to enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP). CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Those who must travel to affected areas of Cabo Delgado, Niassa and Nampula provinces are also advised to consider hiring a security firm. "Avoid all but emergency travel between sunset and sunrise," the advisory says, adding that Americans should "keep a low profile." "Have evacuation plans that do not rely on U.S. government assistance. Have travel documents up to date and easily accessible." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Perry said that, although the advisory highlights serious risks, much of Mozambique remains a beautiful destination for travelers. "On the whole, it's a pretty safe and secure and, as I say, beautiful and enjoyable place to visit," Perry said. "The far north is a dramatic exception." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Fox News Digital reached out to the U.S. State Department for further insights. The warning is one of several travel advisories issued or updated by the State Department in recent months, as officials continue flagging safety concerns for Americans traveling abroad. This month, the State Department issued a Level 2 travel advisory for Ecuador, warning Americans to exercise increased caution due to violent crime, terrorism and kidnapping. articles.title: Charity? Acting? The Cotswolds? What will Harry and Meghan's UK life look like?
articles.summary: The couple's return to the UK is imminent - and what they'll be focusing on here is gradually becoming clearer.
articles.body:
Within the next few days, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex and their two children will have departed California and become residents of the UK.

Since news broke of the move, there has been some confusion as to what British life for Harry and Meghan will look like - but a picture is emerging of the family's priorities.

Over the weekend, there was a deluge of stories about Meghan's return to acting with speculation she would have a role in the next series of The Gentlemen on Netflix, created by British director Guy Ritchie.

Talks are still said to be in the early stages and we understand filming for the third series of the show is imminent - but Netflix has made no comment on who will star, leaving the way open for a former working member of the royal family with an acting background to be cast.

The comedy is about a duke turned drug baron and is mostly filmed in the Cotswolds.

What is clear is that a return to acting more broadly is very much on the agenda for Meghan. It would be financially lucrative for the family in a world of expensive homes, school fees and international travel.

Speaking in June last year to British businesswoman and podcaster Emma Grede, Meghan talked about her Netflix lifestyle series With Love, Meghan, and hinted at a return to acting when asked if she missed that side to her life.

"Sometimes," Meghan replied. "Being back on set with With Love, Meghan was great because I realised how much I miss my crew. I love being around a crew."

But Variety's chief correspondent Marlow Stern says when it comes to deliberations over a potential acting role for Meghan, "a lot of it has to do with scheduling, to be honest".

"They're maybe also negotiating the size of the role and how many days she'll shoot, and also compensation for it. Both sides often play the media to try and push things along, and we could be seeing that."

For Harry, the focus once back in the UK will be on the charity work and patronages he has kept hold of while living thousands of miles away.

He has now completed his final charity engagements in the US before flying back to the UK in the coming days.

In Washington DC, he met military veterans and their families and visited America's main hospital for injured servicemen and women, Walter Reed National Military Medical Centre.

At Arlington National Cemetery, he visited the final resting place of many service personal killed in Iraq and Afghanistan wars where he himself served on two operational tours.

At the grave of Sergeant Michael Verardo, who died last year from complications related to injuries sustained in Afghanistan in 2010, he met Verardo's widow Sarah - who now supports other military families - and their nine-year-old daughter, Elizabeth.

"All my daughter knows about princes or princesses is probably contained to a movie... she whispered to me and said, 'Where is his crown? Did he leave it in the car?'" Sarah said.

"She was very dazzled by the ability to meet him and it made us find bits of sparkle for her at a young age in a very hard experience - and that means a lot to me personally."

It is a reminder of the impact Prince Harry is able to make and what he will hope to bring to an increased amount of public work in the UK.

Plans for a number of charity engagements in September in Britain were already in place.

He will be at the WellChild Awards in London towards the end of the month, continuing his support for the event which honours the bravery of seriously ill children.

There will inevitably be an emphasis on the Invictus Games for wounded service personnel which will be held in Birmingham next July.

In an ideal world, the King, as head of the Armed Forces, would officially open the Games - putting father and son together in public for the first time in several years.

That remains an aspiration from Invictus organisers rather than any definitive plan.

Based in the Cotswolds, settling into school

It's thought the family will base themselves in the Cotswolds. Harry and Meghan previously rented a property there in 2018 and are known to have friends in the area.

Reports that the couple have turned to former Spice Girl Geri Horner and her husband Christian Horner for advice on life in the area have been rejected by Harry and Meghan's official spokesperson.

"Harry and Meghan are great fans of Geri and Christian… the Horners are not advising them on their return, nor have they been asked to do so."

The couple will be back in the UK about a week before the autumn school term begins for their two children, seven-year-old Archie and five-year-old Lilibet. Most terms begin at the end of next week.

It's understood Meghan will concentrate on settling her children into the routine of life in a British school. She is not expected to embark on any kind of full programme of public engagements.

Exploring acting opportunities and running her business, As Ever, will fill her time once her family is settled. She may also appear alongside her husband at some of his charity events.

The couple will keep their multi-million dollar home in Montecito, about a two-hour drive north of Los Angeles. Meghan's mother, Doria Ragland, who has been heavily involved in helping to care for her grandchildren, will remain living in California.

The family is expected to return to the US regularly as well as use the holiday home they have bought near Melides in Portugal.

It is close to a property bought by Princess Eugenie and her husband Jack Brooksbank who have remained close to the Sussexes during the royal fallout.

How involved Harry, Meghan, Archie and Lilibet will be with the wider royal family has not yet been decided.

Over the next few months, several significant royal engagements are in the diary that would involve most senior royals - Remembrance Sunday at the Cenotaph, the Princess of Wales' Carol Service at Westminster Abbey and then Christmas at Sandringham.

Will there be invitations extended to the Sussex family?

Trust remains an issue. There is caution, a degree of wariness and even hostility in some quarters of the Royal Household. These decisions are very much a work in progress.

Harry and Meghan's team has described the move to the UK as being for "an extended period of time".

It is not necessarily a long-term move but may be a chance for the family to experience life in the UK, allowing the children to get to know their grandfather, the King, while they are young enough to not have their education disrupted.

Much of what happens in the months ahead will be a test - of Harry and Meghan's liking for life in the UK, of public reaction to them and of the royal family's ability to continue with their duties alongside the distractions the Sussex family may bring.
