Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) on Sunday warned that it will fine and detain commercial vessels accused of violating its protocols for passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

The PGSA stated on social media that 45 named vessels have been blacklisted and could have their cargoes confiscated.

“Effective immediately, any vessel cooperating with listed vessels … will be added to the list,” the PGSA wrote on the social platform X, adding that the owners of these vessels can submit a formal application to request their removal from the blacklist.

Some of the ships on the PGSA’s blacklist include several ships owned by the United Arab Emirates’s ADNOC Logistics and Services and Saudi Arabia’s national shipping carrier Bahri, Reuters reported .

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned countries on Monday to cut their financial ties with Iran as the U.S. carries out “Operation Economic Outcast,” marketed as an “economic D-Day,” in reference to the U.S. invasion of Normandy Beach in World War II.

“Well, we are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior, why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent responded to a question about the lack of details about the plan.

Bessent said that President Trump was making calls to world leaders, with the Defense, Treasury and State departments contacting their counterparts with the same warning.

Trump hinted at the “economic D-Day” last week, saying it would be a “CRUSHING” economic operation against Iran.

The PGSA was also targeted, with the Treasury Department sanctioning the new body out of Tehran, one of 60 entities, individuals and vessels related to Iran’s nuclear and missile technology programs and its ability to conduct cyber operations and generate oil revenue.

The Trump administration said its goal in going to war with Iran since Feb. 28 was to prevent it from developing and obtaining a nuclear weapon. Iran has retaliated militarily over the last six months while also shutting down the Strait of Hormuz, where roughly 30 percent of the world’s crude oil is exported.

Iran’s hold over the strait has caused global gas prices and inflation to rise. The national average for gas in the U.S. reached $4.09 per gallon on Monday, nearly $1 more than the average last year, according to data from AAA .

Negotiations to reopen the strait and permanently end the war have stalled after both countries initially signed an interim peace deal in June. After a period last month when both countries exchanged strikes, Trump has vowed to crush Iran through economic warfare.

Bessent hinted Sunday that this economic warfare will usher in a final phase of the conflict.

“We are now entering the endgame. At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary,” he wrote on X.

articles.title: Two hours, 500 metres: How Gurgaonâs rain stole my train
articles.summary: Gurgaon rain caused severe waterlogging on Sohna Road, turning a 40-minute trip into a two-hour crawl and making a commuter miss a New Delhi train.
articles.body: GURGAON: I left home in Sector 48 by cab at 1.10pm on Monday to catch a 4.10pm train from New Delhi Railway Station.The plan was to reach the Metro and take Yellow Line to New Delhi. And I thought a three-hour buffer was enough, even by Gurgaon rainy-day standards. I was wrong.The sky had turned cloudy around 11.30am, but the forecast gave no hint of rain. Then, at 12.45pm, it began. By the time my cab arrived at 1.05pm, the roads outside were already waterlogged.Google Maps put the journey to New Delhi Railway Station at one hour 45 minutes â tight, but doable. That estimate meant nothing once we hit Sohna Road.Traffic barely moved. Instead of falling, the ETA kept climbing. After nearly an hour crawling forward, I abandoned the plan to reach the railway station by road and redirected the cab to Millennium City Centre, Yellow Lineâs terminal station, hoping to cover the rest of the distance by Metro. It was barely 6km away, and with the train still two hours off, I thought I had a chance.Gurgaon had other plans.Sohna Road was completely choked. By 3pm, nearly two hours after I had set out, I had covered barely 500 metres, reaching only as far as Subhash Chowk. I turned the cab toward the Metro station anyway, clinging to the hope that I could park and walk in. I couldnât. As 4.10pm came and went, the cab had made it only as far as Sector 47 â nowhere near the Metro, further still from the railway station.The train was gone.Turning back was no easier. Sohna Road remained flooded in stretches, and a journey that should have taken minutes stretched into another ordeal. Sitting in that crawling traffic, one question kept returning: how many others had missed their trains or flights that day, through no fault of their own?There is a difference between missing a train through personal error and missing one because a cityâs roads simply stop functioning after rain. The first is an inconvenience. The second carries a financial cost, a disrupted itinerary and the particular frustration of being stranded by circumstances entirely outside oneâs control.What makes it harder to accept is how familiar it all feels. Every time the city sees heavy rain, the same cycle plays out. Residents flood social media with complaints, authorities promise a waterlogging-free city, officials point to drains being cleared and water being pumped out, and assurances follow that roads will be passable within two or three hours. Then the next spell of rain arrives, and the same roads flood, the same jams return, the same commuters get stranded. Only the promises and explanations change; the experience doesnât.On Monday, I left home three hours before a train that should have taken 40 minutes to reach. Instead, two hours in, I had travelled barely 500 metres. That is not a traffic problem; it is an infrastructure failure that commuters keep paying for, in time, money and disrupted plans.Unless something changes at the root of it, this will not be the last time this city steals someoneâs train or flight after a spell of rain. Zelensky told reporters Russia could draft enough troops next year to reach a total of 500,000, according to Reuters. Russian forces have recently ramped up ballistic missile strikes against Ukraine, targeting…
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday that Russian President Vladimir Putin plans to draft 300,000 more troops in his continued war effort against Ukraine.

Zelensky told reporters Russia could draft enough troops next year to reach a total of 500,000, according to Reuters .

Russian forces have recently ramped up ballistic missile strikes against Ukraine, targeting several cities, including Kyiv. July marked the deadliest month for civilians in Ukraine since May 2022, according to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.

“We see what Putin is doing and what he wants,” Zelensky said Monday on Ukrainian Independence Day, marking 35 years since Ukraine seceded from the Soviet Union.

“A solution to his ballistic terror must be found, and this gamble of his must not pay off,” the Ukrainian leader added, referring to Putin.

To combat the Russian ballistic missile threats, Zelensky has urged the Trump administration to set aside 5 percent of its remaining Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine.

While President Trump granted Ukraine a license to co-produce Patriots in July, analysts have emphasized it will take years before the European nation can produce enough of those weapons to adequately combat Russian ballistics.

The Pentagon has exhausted roughly half of its Patriot missiles during the Iran war, CNN reported earlier this month.

Zelensky has also discussed surging foreign military assistance with other foreign leaders, including during a Monday meeting with European officials, a group Zelensky dubbed the “coalition of the willing.”

“Russia continues its attacks and ballistic missiles — yesterday, we spoke about it, with details. Today we will continue,” Zelensky remarked during the gathering . “So we need to make sure that the winter package of air defense will be in Ukraine.”

“And we need the winter package of Patriot missiles. We hope that we will have this package — we need at least 300 Patriot missiles for the winter and for the cold months.”

As of late July, the U.S. military had between 759 and 827 Patriots, down from 2,330 the day before the Iran conflict began, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies .

Over the last month, the Pentagon has awarded contracts to Northrop Grumman and Lockheed Martin to boost production of Patriot interceptor parts.

articles.title: US formally removes Syria’s designation as State Sponsor of Terrorism
articles.summary: The Trump administration on Monday formally removed Syria from its state sponsor of terrorism (SST) list, an extraordinary milestone for the government of Ahmad al-Sharaa, the former terrorist turned statesman who led the campaign to overthrow the dictatorship of Bashar al-Assad. The removal of the SST designation provides enormous sanctions relief for Syria and the…
articles.body:
The Trump administration on Monday formally removed Syria from its state sponsor of terrorism (SST) list, an extraordinary milestone for the government of Ahmad al-Sharaa, the former terrorist turned statesman who led the campaign to overthrow the dictatorship of Bashar al-Assad.

The removal of the SST designation provides enormous sanctions relief for Syria and the ability for Damascus to fully rejoin the international financial system. The country faces huge challenges in reconstruction following more than a decade of civil war. The U.S. is also delisting al-Sharaa’s group, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), from the specially designated global terrorist (SDGT) list.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the removal of the SST label recognized “positive actions and further commitments” by the Syrian government under al-Sharaa to fully distance the country from acts of international terrorism. Syria was initially put on the list in 1979. Only three other countries are SST — Cuba, Iran and North Korea.

“Rescinding Syria’s designation as an SST and HTS’ designation as an SDGT eliminates the final major barriers for private sector investment in Syria and promotes Syria’s economic recovery and reintegration into the global economy,” Rubio said in a statement.

The World Bank estimated Syria’s reconstruction costs at $216 billion in a report published in October 2025.

On Monday, Trump posted on Truth Social a photo of al-Sharaa and Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani holding the president’s signed executive order that directed sanctions relief on Syria.

Tom Barrack, U.S. ambassador to Turkey and Syria special envoy, described removing the SST designation as ushering in a new era of U.S.-Syrian relations.

“For too long, this designation was another wall separating the Syrian people from the investment, enterprise, and opportunity necessary to rebuild their nation. Today, another wall comes down,” he wrote on social media .

“Capital can replace conflict, enterprise can replace isolation, and commerce can continue to triumph over chaos.”

There is overwhelming bipartisan support for the Trump administration’s sanctions relief on Syria, despite reservations over whether al-Sharaa had shed his terrorist past. Since taking over the country in December 2024, al-Sharaa has renounced his former ties with al Qaeda and the Islamic State and has used close relationships with Turkey and Saudi Arabia to appeal to Trump.

But some lawmakers have raised concern about instances of sectarian violence, Syrian ties with Russia and fair representation in Syria’s new government.

articles.title: Manga-inspired theme park to be built near Paris
articles.summary: The construction of three new parks was given the green light after a €6bn investment from Saudi Arabia.
articles.body:
Three theme parks will be built near Paris as part of a €6bn (£5.13bn) deal agreed between France and Saudi Arabia.

The new development is expected to include a manga-themed park, inspired by the popular Japanese franchise Dragon Ball Z.

French President Emmanuel Macron hailed the move as on a scale not seen "since Disneyland Paris", and added "you know my interest for manga".

An opening date for the parks - which will be built near Cergy-Pontoise - has not been set by the Élysée Palace, but they will open in stages and construction is expected to take years.

The project was given the green light during a two-day state visit to France by Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

It stemmed from a previous discussion between Macron and bin Salman about their shared passion for Japanese comics, "in particular Dragon Ball Z," advisers to the president told reporters on Monday.

Macron is known to be a manga fan and earlier this year ended a press briefing with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi by doing a hand gesture from the Dragon Ball series.

The project will be led by Qiddiya Investment Company (QIC) - part of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund - which previously revealed plans in 2024 to build a Dragon Ball theme park near the country's capital, Riyadh.

According to local reports, the theme parks could be built on the site of the former Mirapolis park in Val-d'Oise, which closed 35 years ago.

But the deal, which the Élysée said would create about 2,000 jobs, also signals deeper ties between France and Saudi Arabia.

The leaders are expected to sign several agreements on health, transport and energy during bin Salman's visit, which will include talks on the US and Iran conflict.

In a post on X on Sunday, Macron said bin Salman's two-day state visit marked an "important milestone".

He added that in the face of challenges in the Middle East, "France and Saudi Arabia have always worked together to promote peace and stability".

Saudi Arabia is aiming to diversify its economy away from its dependence on oil revenues, including via investment in the leisure and entertainment industry.

On Sunday, Macron hosted bin Salman at the closing of the Esports World Cup , which was due to be held in Riyadh but was moved to Paris due to safety concerns over the conflict in the Middle East.

Let peaceful commerce among the nations prevail. And hands off Canada, America’s #1 trading partner, whose people are now boycotting American products because of Trump’s imbecilic policies,” Raskin said in a…
articles.body:
Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) on Sunday went after President Trump for his recent tariffs on Canada.

“Stop Trump’s idiotic trade war killing American businesses. Let peaceful commerce among the nations prevail. And hands off Canada, America’s #1 trading partner, whose people are now boycotting American products because of Trump’s imbecilic policies,” Raskin said in a post on the social platform X.

Raskin’s comments come in the wake of heated trade-related tensions between Washington and Ottawa.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Friday removed Canadian negotiators from trade discussions with the U.S., shortly before the Trump administration’s new set of tariffs went into effect.

A day later, Carney said his country would implement retaliatory tariffs against the U.S.’s new 50 percent tariffs starting Sept. 8.

During a press conference, Carney said Canada would “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses.”

Raskin isn’t the only Democratic critic of the recent U.S. trade tensions with Canada, with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) saying Sunday that Trump is “destroying the relationship with one of our country’s strongest allies.”

“Since Day One, Donald Trump has chosen chaos and cruelty — and by doubling down on his reckless trade war with Canada, he’s further harming our families, farmers, and small business owners,” Shapiro said in a post on X.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: Violence flares in Haiti as gang attack kills 30 people
articles.summary: Island nation grapples with violence as it seeks to hold first elections in more than a decade.
articles.body:
At least 30 people have been killed as a new wave of violence grips Haiti.

A powerful gang coalition mounted the deadly attack on a farming community in Kenscoff, south of the capital, Port-au-Prince, late on Sunday, officials reported. The flare-up in violence comes as Haiti hopes to hold its first general election in more than a decade.

list 2 of 3 Hundreds more displaced as gang violence escalates in Haiti’s capital

list 3 of 3 Photos: Gang violence displaces hundreds in Haiti’s capital

Jean Massillon, Kenscoff’s mayor, said armed men “sowed chaos” as they set homes on fire and killed residents.

He said gang members targeted a church and homes, including that of Jean William Pape, a leading public health expert.

Massillon blamed the attack on members of Viv Ansanm, a group that was designated as a “foreign terrorist organisation” by the United States government last year.

Gangs control an estimated 70 percent of Port-au-Prince. Viv Ansanm has repeatedly targeted Kenscoff, which occupies a strategic position overlooking routes into Petion-Ville, where several embassies, upscale hotels and ⁠the temporary seat of government are located.

A United Nations-backed gang suppression force is mandated to help police fight the gangs and restore order, but it has not yet reached its full capacity of 5,500 members.

According to the UN, gang violence has displaced 1.5 million people across Haiti. The violence has persisted despite efforts to rein it in. More than 3,100 people were reported killed and 1,189 injured from January to June as gangs continued a reign of terror in Port-au-Prince that sparked international concern last year.

Haiti’s prime minister’s office on Monday condemned the “heinous attack” and sought to reassure Haitians that security forces were on high alert and reinforcements were being deployed.

“Kenscoff will not be abandoned,” a statement read. “The government’s authority will be restored, ⁠without weakness and without delay.”

Haitians have been registering to vote in elections planned in January, but experts have warned it’s currently too dangerous to hold the vote.

articles.title: Abbott tells judge Minnesota’s ICE officer extradition lawsuit ‘doomed to fail’
articles.summary: Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) asserted to a judge Monday that he’s not obligated to hand over an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer charged by Mi...
articles.body:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) asserted to a judge Monday that he's not obligated to hand over an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer charged by Minnesota authorities with shooting a Venezuelan man earlier this year during "Operation Metro Surge."

Minnesota is pushing in court to force the extradition of ICE officer Christian Castro, with a key hearing slated for Tuesday. The state insists Abbott has no discretion to avoid signing the warrant.

"In the end, Minnesota's zeal to see Mr. Castro prosecuted on its home turf cannot justify pretermitting Governor Abbott's ongoing deliberations pursuant to the Constitution and state statutes, which are designed to protect against abusive and baseless deprivations of individual liberty," Abbott's lawyers wrote in their formal written response to the court.

U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr., an appointee of President Trump who oversees the case, will consider Minnesota's bid at a Tuesday afternoon hearing in his Brownsville, Texas, courtroom.

It has become a major legal clash between Abbott and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D), who requested Castro's extradition as state authorities charged the ICE officer with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime.

The officer stands accused of injuring a Venezuelan man in the leg by firing a gun at the front door of an occupied Minneapolis home on Jan. 14 amid an immigration enforcement surge in the Twin Cities. Castro had allegedly told investigators he opened fire in self-defense after being hit with a shovel and a broom, only for video footage to undercut the officer's claim.

Abbott has refused to sign a rendition warrant that would pave the way for the officer to return to Minnesota for trial.

In the new filing, the governor's lawyers raised doubts that Castro qualifies for the Constitution's extradition requirement. It demands a state return defendants facing criminal charges who "flee from Justice" when they are "found in another State." Abbott has suggested Castro didn't flee because ICE had ordered him to return to Texas.

"The ordinary meaning of a fugitive entails a volitional act of fleeing, not mere involuntary movement across state lines," his lawyers wrote.

Minnesota insists that Abbott's role is ministerial, and the state wants a judge to immediately pave the way for the officer to be returned.

"The Framers of the Constitution and Congress intended the interstate extradition process to be a swift, summary one in which the state into which a defendant travels promptly returns a fugitive as soon as the requesting state demands it," the state wrote in court filings last week.

Abbott cautioned he hasn't yet made a final decision on the extradition request. But his new filing said that any notion Minnesota could unilaterally enforce the extradition power was "doomed to fail." His filing also took shots at Walz for pardoning a man charged with sexually assaulting a minor.

"Equity favors those with clean hands," Abbott's lawyers wrote.

articles.title: Trump inauguration pastor says Dearborn Christians 'afraid' to speak out in Muslim-majority city
articles.summary: Lorenzo Sewell says Christians in Dearborn, Michigan, privately told him they are afraid to express their faith, accusing city officials of upholding Sharia law.
articles.body: A Detroit pastor who delivered a prayer at President Donald Trump’s inauguration says Christians in Muslim-majority Dearborn, Michigan, have privately told him they are afraid to publicly express their faith, while accusing local officials of giving Muslim residents preferential treatment under a "two-tiered justice system." "Right now, the city officials in Dearborn specifically, they are giving Muslims preferential treatment," Lorenzo Sewell, senior pastor of 180 Church in Detroit, told Fox News Digital in an interview Monday. "Now, how do I know that?" Sewell asked. "This is how I know that. Being a Black man in the city of Detroit, we go to Dearborn. We know that the police know how to enact justice in Dearborn. They know how to pull you over. They know that if they catch you shoplifting, we've had Black women that tried to elude the police and lost their lives in the city of Dearborn." GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS "So, as a Black man that has grown up around Arabs my entire life, I know that the Dearborn police can enact justice," he continued. "So, when someone is being assaulted and nothing happens, when someone's being assaulted and the police choose to look the other way, you can see clearly a two-tiered justice system."  "So, the city council, instead of them renouncing Sharia law, they are actually upholding Sharia law," Sewell added. Sewell recently went viral following remarks he gave at a Dearborn town hall where he said, "America, we have lost this city. This is a city that is no longer up under American laws; we are up under Sharia law. We will not have it anymore." FORT WORTH PRINCIPAL PICK FACES BACKLASH, INVESTIGATION OVER SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS DEFENDING SHARIA LAW CBS News reported last Wednesday that Dearborn police said they made 22 arrests following the "Christian Crusader March," led by conservative activist Jake Lang. Sewell attended the march, which took place near a regularly scheduled Dearborn City Council meeting where he later delivered his viral remarks. In a statement, Dearborn Police Chief Issa Shahin said, "Our officers met a challenging and rapidly evolving situation with the professionalism this community expects, keeping everyone safe, protecting the constitutional rights of those who came to be heard, and allowing the City Council to complete its business. I could not be prouder of them." DOJ WEIGHS CIVIL RIGHTS PROBE INTO FORT WORTH POLICE OVER ALLEGED FIRST AMENDMENT VIOLATIONS Sewell told Fox News Digital he is concerned about the growing presence of what he called Sharia law practices in the community. "One of the examples that I see of Sharia law happening right here in the metro Detroit … in the city of Hamtramck, you are allowed right now to sacrifice animals, literally," Sewell said. "Number two, halal meat. If you go to a public school, you are literally eating meat that's sacrificed to idols, because, according to Sharia law, that's what — that's a lawful meat."  "And I believe the most concerning to me is the call to prayer," he added. "There is no other place in the world that you can go and tell that country, although you are a majority Christian country, you can't go anywhere else in the nation and tell that country they have to change the way they express their religious beliefs." CALIFORNIA LAWMAKERS' PUSH TO MAKE MUSLIM HOLY DAYS STATE HOLIDAYS SPARKS DEBATE OVER SCHOOL NEUTRALITY In January 2023, the Hamtramck City Council voted to allow animal sacrifice, and the website for Dearborn Public Schools says, "Dearborn Public Schools ensures all meats served in our schools are certified Halal." The certificate for the halal meat, partially in Arabic, reads in part, "We certify that the food processing facility of Saad Wholesale, Inc. in Detroit, MI, USA has been inspected and approved by our Islamic organization for processing, packing, and labeling of Halal Meat & Poultry Products by applying our procedures according to the Islamic Rites." "I see the city council upholding Sharia law through things like the call to prayer, through things like halal meat, through having more Arab writing than they do actually English, by having the chief of police talk more about protecting the rules of Islam and Islamic leaders instead of protecting the rights of all Americans," Sewell continued. "So you can see clearly when someone speaks freely, they can be attacked, and it'd be justified," he added. "I can give you a clear example. My wife had her life threatened. We had the guy's number, we had his address, we had everything, and the lieutenant did absolutely nothing. So, that's how you can see a two-tier justice system." DEI HIRING BOOST FOR ONE BLUE STATE'S MUSLIM COMMISSION INITIATIVE FLIES IN FACE OF TRUMP'S ANTI-WOKE PUSH He also claimed that Christians in the area feel afraid to express their faith. "Since I went viral, I've had Dearborn Christians come out from the north, south, east, and west, and they're afraid," Sewell said. "I want you to think about this for a moment, America. Think about being in a Christian nation, being afraid to talk about Christ. I want you to just think about that for a moment." "I'm having people say, 'I'm with you, but I'm afraid to say it,'" he continued. "'I'm with you, but I'm afraid to be by you.' 'I'm with you —' This is how we know we are in a two-tiered system because, in a Christian nation, we're afraid to be Christians." TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS Dearborn city council president Mike Sareini told Fox News Digital that the pastor’s claims are false. "The City of Dearborn is an American city governed by the U.S. Constitution, the laws of the State of Michigan, and the City of Dearborn Charter," Sareini said. "Those laws apply equally to every resident, regardless of religion or background. Everyone is treated the same." "There is no evidence of preferential treatment for any religious group. These accusations are unfounded, and I challenge anyone to present evidence otherwise," Sareini continued. "Dearborn is home to approximately 30 churches and 10 mosques," he added. "Most recently, pastors from throughout Dearborn spoke at a press conference and publicly confirmed that people of different faiths live together peacefully in Dearborn, without the conflict being alleged." articles.title: US set for largest mass visa revocation in history targeting up to 200,000 foreigners, officials say
articles.summary: The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asyl...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the United States. If it happens, the move would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in U.S. history and would likely face legal challenges.

Unless challenged or revised, the State Department is expected to announce in the coming weeks the revocation of so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, according to State Department documents obtained by The Associated Press and two U.S. officials. The action will be taken in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security.

"We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," said State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott.

He declined to comment on the number of visas that might be revoked, saying "as the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis."

The revocations would not necessarily result in their immediate deportation, the officials said. Most of those with asylum cases currently pending would be recategorized but would lose their status as business or tourism travelers, according to the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the revocations are not final yet.

Since President Donald Trump took office for his second term last year, his administration has steadily ramped up restrictions on visa applicants — demanding more information about their social media histories, requiring the posting of expensive bonds for the processing of visas, and outright banning the issuance of visas to citizens of certain countries.

In a social media post on Monday, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau called out people who he said try to use tourist and business visas to get into the United States and then apply for asylum.

"People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims," Landau wrote on X. "Asylum isn't supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law." Landau cited the case of a Colombian citizen who came to the U.S. in 2015 on a tourist visa and then applied for asylum.

B1 visas are generally issued for business trips and B2 visas are generally issued for tourism, family visits or medical care. It was not immediately clear from the documents or the officials how many of these visa holders are seeking or have sought asylum in the United States and would be affected by the revocations.

Current applicants for B1 and B2 visas are asked to affirm that they will not apply for asylum in the United States and prove that they intend to return to their home countries.

In the past 18 months, the State Department has revoked about 175,000 visas for people who have been convicted or accused of crimes ranging from drunken driving to rape and robbery, as well as for people who have spoken out publicly against U.S. policies, particularly in the Middle East.

The administration has also moved to crack down on so-called birth tourism, a practice the administration claims is used by foreign pregnant women to come to the United States to give birth so that their child will benefit from birthright citizenship . Trump has tried several times to end birthright citizenship, but those challenges have been rejected by courts, including the Supreme Court.

The State Department documents obtained by the AP suggest screening of current B1 and B2 visa holders began after the State Department received information about asylum requests from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

articles.title: Ambush in South Sudan kills peacekeeping troops
articles.summary: Armed men injured three additional peacekeepers as fears grow of the country relapsing into civil war.
articles.body:
An ambush has killed two United Nations peacekeepers in South Sudan.

The UN Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) said in a statement issued on Monday that armed men had ambushed a patrol as it travelled toward Pajut in Jonglei state. The attack comes as fears persist that the country risks sliding into a full-scale civil war.

list 3 of 3 US courts clear way for deportations of South Sudan, Myanmar nationals

The identities and nationalities of those killed have not yet been disclosed. Three other peacekeepers were wounded, along with two South Sudanese police officers and two civilian staff attached to the mission.

The UN peacekeeping mission said it deployed a “Quick Reaction Force” to secure the area and support the emergency response.

“Such deadly violence targeting UNMISS personnel, who are serving to support peace in South Sudan, is unacceptable,” Anita Kiki Gbeho, the head of the mission, said.

Numerous attacks on humanitarian workers have been recorded this year as the prospect of full-blown civil war rises, but violence against peacekeepers is rare.

UN figures show more than 450 attacks on humanitarian workers and assets between January and July, more than double last year’s total for the same period. At least 36 humanitarian workers and contractors were killed, surpassing the 31 killed across 2025.

The violence is playing out against months of grinding conflict between government troops and forces loyal to opposition leader Riek Machar.

Once vice president, Machar was suspended from the post last year and now sits under house arrest, facing treason charges he says are politically motivated.

His 2018 power-sharing agreement with President Salva Kiir has fallen apart, and South Sudan now finds itself edging toward a full civil war – a situation the deal was struck eight years ago to avoid.

Fighting escalated in December, when opposition forces seized government outposts in Jonglei. The government has hit back with air strikes and ground assaults, even as it insists it remains committed to the 2018 accord.

The United States, for its part, has kept pushing Kiir and Machar toward talks, calling earlier this year for “urgent action to uphold peace and mitigate the risk of civil war through an immediate return to dialogue among the parties to the 2018 peace agreement.”

articles.title: Ceasefire monitoring mission arrives in Democratic Republic of Congo
articles.summary: Fighting persists in the mineral-rich region despite ceasefire agreements.
articles.body:
A monitoring mission has been deployed in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to verify the formal ceasefire between the DRC’s army and M23 rebels said to be backed by Rwanda.

The United Nations and government sources said on Monday that the monitoring team had arrived to track the progress of the Qatari-mediated truce . Despite the agreement to end the hostilities, fighting has continued on the ground.

list 2 of 3 DR Congo files case against Rwanda at ICJ over decades of alleged ‘abuses’

list 3 of 3 DR Congo, M23 rebels agree on roadmap for peace talks

The UN said that the mission had deployed to Minembwe, located in the country’s mineral-rich South Kivu province, where intense fighting has persisted in recent months.

The Swiss government announced on Sunday that the DRC and M23 had agreed on a roadmap for peace talks after closed-door negotiations, and that a mission would be deployed to verify violations of the ceasefire agreement signed in Doha, Qatar in July 2025.

The mission is composed of members of the Congolese government and M23, as well as observers from member countries of the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR).

Local journalists reported that the UN Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of Congo (MONUSCO) provided logistical support for the deployment.

The mission will visit Uvira, from where the M23 withdrew in January, as well as Kalehe, where fighting has been reported in recent weeks.

Multiple armed groups have fought over the DRC’s mineral-abundant eastern provinces, including the Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC) and M23, which seized swathes of territory and advanced on Goma, the capital of the North Kivu province, last year.

Peace efforts led by Qatar and the United States have sought to end the crisis, leading to the signing of two separate accords.

DRC President Felix Tshisekedi and Rwandan President Paul Kagame – whose country has been accused of backing the M23 rebels – signed a “historic” peace and economic agreement in December aimed at ending fighting, five months after the two agreed to a ceasefire. However, fighting has continued on the ground.

Both sides have accused the other of alleged abuses and ceasefire violations.

In a statement on Monday, the DRC condemned alleged M23 “crimes and serious rights violations” in territory under its control, accusing the group of killing “more than 300 people” in June and July.

The M23 has rejected the accusations. A spokesperson for the group said on X that government forces had launched a “deadly attack” with artillery on a village near Minembwe.

articles.title: U.S. removes Syria from terrorism sponsor list, lifting major investment obstacle
articles.summary: Monday’s announcement also delisted the Nusrah Front as a terrorist group, leaving Cuba, Iran and North Korea as the three countries Washington designates as state sponsors of terrorism.
articles.body: The United States removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism on Monday, lifting what Damascus says was the last major impediment to investing in the country as Washington deepens ties to the new Syrian government. The removal, posted on the U.S. Treasury’s website, took effect after a 45-day congressional review period triggered when President Donald Trump formally notified Congress on July 8 of his intention to rescind the designation. “These actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement. Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani told Reuters on Saturday that the government hoped removing what he called the “last obstacle” would help reconnect Syria to the global financial and economic system and boost investment. “There is no longer any obstacle to investment, doing business and rebuilding economic life in Syria,” he said. Syria had been on the list since 1979, when Washington accused the government of former President Hafez al-Assad of supporting militant groups. The designation remained throughout the rule of his son Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled by rebels led by current President Ahmed al-Sharaa in December 2024. Cuba, Iran, North Korea remain Monday’s announcement also removed the designation of the Nusrah Front as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organization, leaving Cuba, Iran and North Korea as the three countries designated by Washington as state sponsors of terrorism. The designation carries restrictions on U.S. foreign assistance, defense exports and sales, certain dual-use items and financial transactions, and had remained a major deterrent for banks and investors even after Washington dismantled its broader sanctions program on Syria. Trump’s administration terminated comprehensive U.S. sanctions on Syria in July 2025, while maintaining targeted sanctions against Assad and his associates, rights abusers, drug traffickers, Islamic State and al Qaeda affiliates and Iranian proxies. The U.S. Treasury has since said American financial institutions can provide services to Syria, process payments involving Syrian banks and establish correspondent banking relationships with them, provided sanctioned parties are not involved. But the terrorism designation remained a source of legal and compliance risk for firms considering entering Syria, whose government is seeking billions of dollars in investment to rebuild after nearly 14 years of war. Signs of interest had grown ahead of the removal. Syria’s Finance Ministry said this month that Finance Minister Mohammad Yisr Barnieh held talks with Bank of America executives over potential cooperation and Syria’s reintegration into the international financial system. Bank officials expressed willingness to visit Syria and continue discussions, according to the ministry. Mastercard has gone further, announcing in May that it was working with QNB Group and Syria’s central bank to prepare infrastructure for international card payments in the country. The company has described itself as an early investor in Syria and said it wants to help connect Syrian consumers and businesses to global payment networks. Continued cooperation Trump notified Congress of his decision after meeting Sharaa in Ankara in July, telling the Syrian president in a letter seen by Reuters that he had promised to “remove all barriers” preventing Syria from rebuilding. The delisting also followed months of negotiations between Damascus and Washington over Syria’s economic and foreign policy. Reuters reported this month that Damascus agreed to drastically reduce imports of Russian oil during discussions with Washington over lifting the terrorism designation, according to three sources familiar with the talks. Trump has increasingly embraced Sharaa, the former commander of al Qaeda’s Nusra Front who broke ties with the global jihadist network in 2016 and led the rebel coalition that overthrew Assad. Washington has praised cooperation by Sharaa’s government against the Islamic State and said easing restrictions is intended to give Syria an opportunity to stabilize, attract investment and rebuild.

articles.title: US-Canada trade war heats up as Trump threatens to hike auto tariffs
articles.summary: Mark Carney accused Trump of wanting to "destroy" Canada's auto industry, and said he would only resume trade talks if the US comes with the "right attitude".
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has threatened to hike US tariffs on automobiles originating in Canada, as the trade war between the two neighbours continues to heat up.

Trump said on Monday that he will increase tariffs on Canadian cars and trucks, as well as auto parts, from 25% to 50% as of 1 January.

It comes after US-Canada trade talks collapsed late last week, with each side accusing the other of making unreasonable last-minute demands.

Late on Monday, Canada officials announced a news conference on Tuesday where they would outline how the country would respond to the trade war and work to "protect and support Canadian workers and businesses during these challenging times".

The news conference at 11:00 ET (16:00 BST) will include government leaders in business, finance and economic development.

Earlier in the day, Prime Minister Mark Carney called Trump's latest levy threat unsurprising and accused the president of wanting to destroy Canada's auto industry. He added that Canada is ready to resume talks only if the US comes with the "right attitude".

The war of words followed several US and Canadian officials saying that talks were suspended with no set date to resume.

Canada walked away from trade negotiations late on Friday night, moments before a US-imposed deadline that would add a 50% levy on nearly $20bn (C$28bn; £14bn) of Canadian imports.

The collapse in talks marked a significant change in tone from earlier in the week, when both sides appeared optimistic that a new US-Canada trade deal could be reached.

Canadian officials have said the US introduced last-minute demands that were "unacceptable", including a clause limiting which countries Canada could sign trade deals with.

US officials, meanwhile, said it was Canada that introduced last-minute changes.

"They wanted more," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in an interview with CNBC on Monday.

The breakdown led to growing tensions as both sides publicly dug in their heels.

On Monday, Trump's tariff threats to Canada's auto industry followed Carney declaring the country would counter his levies with reciprocal tariffs on US goods "dollar for dollar".

'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war

How Canada could hit back to hurt the US economy - and Trump

Trump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapse

Carney said he was focused on supporting Canadian businesses impacted by new 50% US tariffs after the Friday deadline expired, as well as building infrastructure to diversify Canada's trade, which historically has relied heavily on the US.

Carney announced funding of C$11bn ($7.95bn; £5.83bn) to build six icebreakers at a Quebec shipyard for the Canadian Coast Guard that will replace its medium and heavy ageing fleet.

The icebreakers will be used to open winter shipping routes through Canada's northern and Atlantic waters.

Meanwhile, Ontario's outspoken premier, Doug Ford, whose province is home to Canada's auto manufacturing industry, responded to Trump's tariffs and threats by telling the US president to "kiss my ass".

Ford also suggested that Canada should charge the US extra for its oil and gas, as well as electricity and critical minerals, adding that he will be speaking to Carney on ways to "fight back".

His comments appeared to catch the attention of Trump, who in a Truth Social post accused Ford of "bluster" and wrote: "Someone should get these clowns to 'fall in line' or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!".

Canada accounts for 60% of total US crude oil imports and close to 100% of US natural gas exports, according to Canadian government data.

Businesses on both sides have warned that they stand to be hurt by the new wave of US tariffs on Canada, as well as the retaliatory tariffs that Canada plans to impose on 8 September.

In Portland, Oregon, Mike Roach and Kim Osgood, owners of Paloma Clothing say the price of one of their best-selling items - specially designed pillows made in Canada - could shoot up by around 50% to $90. For now, they are holding out on keeping the prices steady, hoping that the "tariff problem" is worked out soon, said Roach.

"It would be one thing if we had three months' notice - that would be something you could plan around, do some work with the vendors," he said. "But when it happens literally overnight you're really stuck."

The rapidly escalating trade war is also raising questions about the other country in North America - Mexico - and the trade pact between the three neighbours known as the USMCA.

Both Canada and Mexico have said they want the USMCA extended for another 16 years, but the US has said it will not renew in its current form. The pact underpins $1.6tn in North American Trade.

Escalating trade tensions mean "the risk of the USMCA unravelling has increased", experts from the Oxford Economics forecasting firm warned on Monday. That, in turn, "would plunge Canada into recession and leave it on a permanently lower growth path".

Carney faces crucial test after walking away from Trump's deal

articles.title: Ontario’s Ford warns US power could be cut as he trades insults with Trump
articles.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford on Monday threatened to cut the province’s power exports to the U.S. as a trade war with President Trump plays out publicly for a second time. Ford told reporters “everything is on the table” when it comes to retaliatory measures against the White House in response to failed trade talks and…
articles.body:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford on Monday threatened to cut the province’s power exports to the U.S. as a trade war with President Trump plays out publicly for a second time.

Ford told reporters “everything is on the table” when it comes to retaliatory measures against the White House in response to failed trade talks and heightened tariffs .

“We power 1.5 million homes and businesses. Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes,” Ford said at a Monday press conference.

“You won’t get a grain of sand out of Ontario,” he added.

Ontario’s power grid connects directly across the border to Michigan, New York and Minnesota. Ford has previously threatened to cut power to U.S. states during the fallout of trade negotiations last year.

Ultimately, at that time, he met with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and cooled tensions via bilateral talks.

However, pressures have resumed after Trump introduced a 50 percent tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods.

Ottawa had already said it would respond with retaliatory tariffs before Ford launched his energy threat and proposed pulling U.S. access to Canada’s critical minerals.

Trump responded to the potential actions on Truth Social and called Ford the “overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford,” Doug’s older brother who served on city council and as mayor of Toronto.

The president said Canada was facing “bad leadership” primarily from Prime Minister Mark Carney and “Flunky Ford.”

He urged the two to “fall in line,” to which Ford said , “kiss my a‑‑.”

Canadian opposition leader Pierre Poilievre is urging politicians to tread lightly with the Trump administration.

“As Canadians are vulnerable to an escalating trade war with the United States, Parliament must be reconvened. Canadians deserve answers on how trade talks collapsed, what tariffs will cost their families, and how their jobs will be protected,” Poilievre, the leader of Canada’s Conservative Party in the Canadian Parliament, said Monday in a post on the social platform X .

articles.title: Zelensky says wartime election would ‘destroy’ Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday that holding elections amid Russia’s war with Ukraine would “destroy” the country. “I believe that ​if we want to destroy the country, then we can move towards elections ​during this kind of war,” Zelensky told reporters. The president said elections “in general pose major risks,” noting that holding an…
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday that holding elections amid Russia’s war with Ukraine would “destroy” the country.

“I believe that ​if we want to destroy the country, then we can move towards elections ​during this kind of war,” Zelensky told reporters.

The president said elections “in general pose major risks,” noting that holding an election “right now would be a tsunami for the state, one that would divide Ukraine,” Politico reported .

“That’s why my strategy is to steer the country toward an ending of the war and to preserve an ⁠independent ​and sovereign state,” he added.

Ukrainian law bars the country from holding elections during wartime.

Polling released by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology earlier this month found that 57 percent of Ukrainians want to hold elections after the war ends.

Zelensky’s remarks come after ousted former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for a wartime poll in an address last week, NBC News reported. Zelensky said he thought some of Fedorov’s actions were misguided.

“I really had and still have a very positive attitude toward Mykhailo,” the president said. “We have been through a lot together. But I believe that he himself goes, or is pushed, into the wrong things.”

He appeared to link Fedorov to a meeting involving Starlink and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, where Fedorov told Zelensky that SpaceX agreed to have Ukraine use Starlink on Russian territory. Zelensky raised this with President Trump and later told him that Musk rejected the proposal, accusing him of having misled Trump.

Zelensky said that this incident was among the reasons behind “some of the steps” that led to Fedorov no longer being in his position.

Fedorov has emerged as a rival to Zelensky, telling Ukrainians Tuesday that the “people cannot endlessly live in a state where they do not understand why certain decisions are made,” Politico reported.

The former minister doubled down on his address during a Sunday interview with the BBC . He told the outlet that Zelensky has “questions to answer” about corruption within the government. Fedorov also talked about Ukrainian elections, noting that “democracy should not be the hostage of” Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“If I cannot share my ideas and be open about them with my own society, then what are we fighting for?” he told the broadcaster.

Zelensky was first elected in 2019, when he defeated incumbent President Petro Poroshenko in a landslide victory. He was a comedian and television personality before entering politics.

He said last December that Ukraine was ready for elections after Trump had said the same thing.

“Since this question is raised today by the president of the United States of America, our partners, I will answer very briefly,” Zelensky told U.S. reporters at the time after a phone call with Trump. “Look, I am ready for elections. … I personally have the will and readiness to do this.”

articles.title: Kit Harington replaces Nicholas Hoult as Gilderoy Lockhart in HBO's Harry Potter series
articles.summary: Hoult was announced as Gilderoy Lockhart two weeks ago but has dropped out due to scheduling issues.
articles.body:
Kit Harington is joining the highly anticipated Harry Potter TV series as the wizarding world's celebrity-turned-Hogwarts instructor Gilderoy Lockhart.

X-Men star Nicholas Hoult was originally cast in the second series earlier this month but has now left due to scheduling issues, according to HBO.

Best known for playing Jon Snow in Game of Thrones, Harington also appears in BBC and HBO financial drama Industry. The star previously voiced Lockhart in an audio version of Harry Potter.

"I'm a huge Potter fan. I've got to be honest, he's one of my favourite characters," Harington told Collider . "So, to be offered to play him is a real dream. I've had a taste of him [in the audiobook] and felt my way around him. He's just a wonderful creation."

Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone is due to premiere this Christmas on HBO Max.

Season two will adapt the second book in the series by JK Rowling, The Chamber of Secrets, which chronicles Potter's second year at the magical school.

"Before we begin year two at Hogwarts, there has been a slight change due to schedule: Kit Harington will be stepping into the role of Gilderoy Lockhart," an HBO statement said .

The new series adaptation of the best-selling books stars newcomer Dominic McLaughlin as the boy wizard, Alastair Stout as his best friend Ron Weasley and Arabella Stanton as the young witch Hermione Granger.

Oscar-nominated actor Jon Lithgow has been cast as Hogwarts headmaster Albus Dumbledore and Nick Frost will play gamekeeper Rubeus Hagrid.

The show could reunite Harington, who has said he is a lifelong fan of the books, with director and producer Mark Mylod, who worked on Game of Thrones and is directing some Harry Potter episodes. Mylod is an executive producer on the new series along with author JK Rowling.

Lockhart was portrayed in the Harry Potter films by Kenneth Branagh, and is a key character in Rowling's second book in the hugely successful book series.

The vain wizard, who authored several books on his purported encounters with dark creatures, serves as Hogwarts' latest professor for the defence against the dark arts and fancies himself as a mentor to Harry in his second year.

Hoult, along with other cast members, has faced some backlash for his decision to join the show from those who are opposed to Rowling's views on gender identity and trans rights.

Representatives for Harington and Hoult did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The HBO series is expected to take 10 years to complete, as producers plan multiple seasons covering each of Rowling's seven books, which the eight blockbuster films were originally based on.

articles.title: China's humanoid robots are stealing the show, but a quieter machine revolution is unfolding
articles.summary: There are more than two million robots working in China's factories - and they are scaling up fast.
articles.body:
"I take a nap and the world changes," says Chen Tianyu.

His world certainly does. The 28-year-old keeps up with the latest technology by spending his spare time in factories that are switching to automation. That way he knows what to prioritise when teaching his class about artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics.

In front of him, around 30 college students are studying code. One of them is typing furiously as his eyes dart from the screen to the robot: "The idea is it will grab that cylindrical piece and move it over there."

A line of industrial robots are waiting to be programmed, and in another part of the classroom, students are trying to develop robotic medical instruments. As he guides them, Chen declares: "If you are not needed by the world of AI and robotics, then you'll definitely be among those eliminated".

For the people in this room, this is a step - or rather a leap - towards a future that China is meticulously building: Xi Jinping's $20bn (£14.7bn) plan to put his country at the forefront of innovation and in direct competition with the US.

The evidence is all around them. They are in the Hangzhou Technician Institute, one of several huge, purpose-built vocational schools that want to churn out the next generation of tech-savvy engineers. The campus sits on the outskirts of Hangzhou, a former imperial capital whose futuristic skyline is just the first hint of its role as a global tech hub.

Across the country, there are more than two million robots working in China's factories - which is more than anywhere else - and they are continuing to scale up at extraordinary speed.

It is a commitment that will surely change the world, much like the last time the Chinese economy underwent a massive transformation. It is already shipping its robots across the globe: more than half of the world's industrial robots are now made in China.

What is less clear is the impact of such sweeping automation in a country that sits at the heart of global manufacturing, trade and innovation. What does this mean for China's human workforce, for instance? And how would we be able to truly measure the cost of this transformation in a regime that controls information so tightly?

The future of China's workers is uncertain in the industrial revolution the world has been watching: gleaming solar grids, peak hours made noiseless by electric vehicles, machines that run faster than Usain Bolt. Over the weekend, China hosted the second edition of the World Humanoid Games where robots boxed, sprinted and marched.

What is fuelling this spectacle is another, less visible revolution happening inside factories and classrooms.

The BBC has visited industrial sites where we have been shown robots that do not look human, or dance or leap on stage but weld, paint, lift, assemble and work around the clock without a break or benefits. Some are designed to build more robots. We have also been inside academies where China is training the people who will work alongside its robotic workforce.

This is a front-row seat to what Xi calls China's "new productive forces" - and how they could reshape the country.

On a factory floor in the southern city of Chengdu, the old and and the new are working side by side.

An assembly line of around 30 middle-aged men and women is screwing, drilling and polishing CRP Technology's signature product: a robotic arm which performs various industrial tasks. Also in the room are four young engineers crowded around a console, trying to crack the code for a prototype, a new robot that they hope will help build other robots.

One of them, 31-year-old Pang Kai, who is part of the research and development team, pushes the sleek skeleton across the room. Because China's future workforce is not quite ready to strut out. For now, it can only do simple repetitive movements, such as scan a QR code.

"Maybe in another half year, it can do another task," Pang says, smiling wistfully. It's a long road and the team are celebrating every small win.

CRP Technology, which employs around 300 people, has been building robot arms for nine years. Each arm can be tailored to a factory's needs to help build cars, electronics or wind turbines. The firm says a single arm can be programmed to perform more than 90% of repetitive tasks.

The engineers also wonder if, one day, they can replace the company's workforce. "We want our new robot to be like human beings. We hope it can think by itself," says Pang. "We need these kinds of robots because maybe in 10 years, we won't have enough workers in China."

A shrinking population and an ageing workforce is another reason Beijing is in a hurry to revolutionise its factories. By 2035, more than a third of China's population will be over 60, according to official estimates. The country will also lose nearly 60 million people in the next decade - almost equivalent to the population of France - according to some estimates.

The hope is that increased automation will fill this looming gap in the workforce before it starts to affect an already sluggish economy. But the speed of the transition is key. Around 120 million people still work in the manufacturing sector. If China moves too quickly, job losses could follow dealing a catastrophic blow to millions who depend on factory wages.

"In theory, machines can work 24 hours a day, which is certainly an advantage compared with human workers. But machines also require maintenance. Every day we need time for that, and each month the production line also requires inspection and repair," says Cao Li, vice-president of EV maker Leapmotor.

Increasingly popular in Europe and the UK, the company's budget-friendly, tech-focused cars come together at the Hangzhou factory with robots aiding the process at every step. At the end of the assembly line, more humans emerge.

The company has more than 25,000 workers and hundreds of them make the final checks as the sparkling new vehicles roll past. Will there be a day when they are no longer needed?

"It's entirely possible," Cao says. "And it may come relatively quickly. In workshops, including stamping, welding, and painting, we've basically achieved 100% automation."

China has the edge over the US due to its enormous manufacturing base. Motors, batteries, electronics, gears, sensors - everything needed to build the body of a robot is all at hand.

"China also has an idea. It has a plan. They know where they want to be in five years. They plan at a top level, but they break it down to the regions, to the municipalities," says Dr Susanne Bieller, General Secretary of the International Federation of Robotics.

"If you want to build a robot in Shenzhen - there's an entire ecosystem. It takes you less than one hour to source the components you need to make a robot. In Europe it can take you up to a week."

However, she acknowledges that while China is good at building the body, the US is still leading at building the "brain", which includes developing the AI to programme robots. And yet Chinese firms, from DeepSeek to Moonshot, have been unveiling new AI models that they say can compete with top US firms.

Driven by an "open-source" approach, where AI start-ups share their code, Chinese innovation has been able to catch up faster than expected, despite US export controls over critical advanced chips. Analysts now believe that the next leg of this race will be determined not by who has the best language model, but who can put this intelligence into millions of machines.

And that is why China is also investing in producing a generation of students learning to imagine what could come next.

At the Hangzhou Technician Institute, for example, children can start from the age of 15. And the scale of what is being taught can feel staggering. There is an entire building dedicated to engines and aeronautics, and a restricted floor for students who will work to keep China at the forefront of processing rare earths - another crucial commodity in the battle with Washington.

Some see this as a solution to China's stubbornly high youth unemployment rate, with one in five struggling to find a job. "Our students are in demand and can even be pre-booked by companies. They don't need to worry about employment at all, and we hold competitions as part of their training," Chen, the young teacher, says.

"It's better to find your position within the technological wave. In the process of progress, structural changes are bound to occur, and these structural changes are exactly where students' future employment opportunities lie."

But China still faces serious economic challenges, from a property crisis that continues to drag on to huge local government debt and persistently low consumption.

It is unclear if and how the revolution Beijing is touting will fix these, and it is hard to gauge how those whose jobs are threatened feel about the change that is coming. Will robots create prosperity for them, or simply take many of their jobs?

"My students ask me what will happen in the future," Chen says. "I say I don't know. Technology is changing so fast. But we can't just stand still and sleep here. We have to move forward to see what we are capable of doing."

articles.title: Lockerbie bombing trial postponed days before it was due to start
articles.summary: The trial of a Libyan man is delayed for a third time, after new evidence on the 37-year-old case came to light three days ago.
articles.body:
The trial of a Libyan man over the Lockerbie bombing has been postponed for a third time, after new evidence on the 37-year-old case came to light three days ago.

Jury selection was due to get under way in Washington DC on Wednesday but the BBC understands a new start date has been set for January next year.

Lawyers acting for Abu Agila Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi said "newly discovered evidence" previously unknown to the defence and prosecutors from the US government emerged on Friday 21 August.

Al-Marimi has denied building the bomb that destroyed Pan Am Flight 103 on 21 December 1988, killing 270 people.

His lawyers told the court: "Constitutional and ethical obligations require the defence to investigate this development."

They said they met Al-Marimi on Sunday and he agreed that they should ask for the postponement.

The trial judge, Dabney Friedrich, has agreed that the start date should be set aside, underlining the potential importance of the new evidence.

She would have been extremely reluctant to allow an 11th hour postponement after months of preparation and marathon pre-trial legal battles.

For the relatives of those who died and Al-Marimi himself, this latest delay means a verdict might not come until next spring.

It is yet another stunning development in a saga that has witnessed countless twists and turns over nearly four decades.

Pan Am 103 was flying from Heathrow to New York when the bomb exploded in its forward hold, breaking the plane apart at 31,000 feet.

All 259 passengers and crew on board were killed. Another 11 people died in Lockerbie when the wreckage fell on their homes.

Of the victims, 190 were American and 43 from the UK.

Nearly four decades later, the bombing remains the worst terror attack and mass murder in British history.

Al-Marimi has been in US custody since 2022 and was originally due to stand trial in May 2025.

That date was set aside following a joint request from the prosecution and defence, who cited the complexity of the case and Al-Marimi's ill health.

The trial was pencilled in for April this year but was called off again, after the defence asked for more time to prepare.

The Lockerbie bombing has been the subject of a joint Scottish-US investigation since December 1988.

Prosecutors from the Crown Office and detectives from Police Scotland were due to travel to Washington to attend the case, and Scottish witnesses were expected to be among the first to give evidence at the trial.

Laura Buchan, head of the Lockerbie investigation team at the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service said: "I recognise that this adjournment will be disappointing for the families and for those who have followed this case over many years.

"As the matter remains before the court, it would not be appropriate to comment on the reasons for the adjournment.

"Although these proceedings are being led by the United States authorities, Scottish prosecutors and police officers remain fully committed to supporting the pursuit of justice."

Campaigner Kara Weipz, who is president of the Victims of Pan Am Flight 103 group, said she was "floored" when she received the news that the trial had been postponed.

She told the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast programme that she would pray that older relatives of victims would "remain healthy" so they can see the trial eventually take place.

She said: "It's always been my goal for as many family members to be able to witness this trial as possible and to gain more of the truth.

"If that's what this evidence brings, that's what the families have been fighting for for almost four decades - we want the truth, we want to know what happened - and if that's what this brings then this time will be worth it."

Dr Jim Swire, who has campaigned for justice since his daughter, Flora, was killed in the bombing, said he believed the delay in the trial could be beneficial if it meant more care would be taken over evidence.

He said: "For many years, we've been after only one thing, and that is the truth.

"If each delay allows the court to assemble more of the true evidence, I am all in favour of it.

"The judge seems to have stuck her oar in and insisted on further care being taken about the assembly of evidence, and if so, that is good news."

A grandfather in his 70s, Al-Marimi has been accused of carrying out the attack along with two Libyans who faced a Scottish court in May 2000.

Three judges heard the case at Camp Zeist, a former US air force base in the Netherlands.

After eight months, they ruled the atrocity was an act of state sponsored terrorism carried out by members of the Libyan intelligence service.

On 21 December 1988, a plane explodes over Lockerbie, Scotland, killing 270 people. Almost four decades on, there's fresh evidence. Who was really behind the bombing?

The judges convicted one of the Libyans, Abdulbasset Al-Megrahi, of mass murder and jailed him for life.

He died from cancer in 2012, after being freed on compassionate grounds by the Scottish government.

The Scottish Criminal Cases Review Commission twice referred Megrahi's case to the appeal court but the conviction was upheld .

The second Libyan, Al Amin Khalifah Fhimah was acquitted and returned home to a hero's welcome in Tripoli.

The US government says Al-Marimi admitted bombing the plane along with Megrahi and Fhimah when he was questioned in a Libyan detention facility in 2012.

The alleged confession was handed to Scottish investigators in 2017 and is now central to the prosecution case.

Al-Marimi has claimed the confession is false and was made under duress, but judge Friedrich ruled it can be admitted as evidence at the trial.

articles.title: North Carolina doctor accused of shooting 2 sisters in alleged interstate road rage attack
articles.summary: North Carolina doctor Richard Thomas Arriviello allegedly shot two sisters in a Jeep on Interstate 77 during a road rage incident before fleeing.
articles.body: A North Carolina doctor was arrested Aug. 22 after he allegedly fired into a Jeep during an interstate road rage incident, wounding two sisters, ages 12 and 20, according to Virginia State Police. Dr. Richard Thomas Arriviello, 61, of Charlotte, North Carolina, was driving north on Interstate 77 in his Mercedes-Benz around 8:50 a.m. when gunfire erupted about three miles north of the North Carolina-Virginia state line. State police said in a press release that Arriviello fired into the moving Jeep, striking both sisters in the legs. Both victims were airlifted to a hospital with injuries that were not considered life-threatening, according to police. 'TESLA ROAD RAGE DRIVER' SENTENCED TO SEVEN YEARS IN PRISON AFTER ATTACKING MOTHER AND DAUGHTER IN HAWAII Arriviello then fled in his Mercedes-Benz, police said. Troopers spotted and stopped the Mercedes-Benz about 15 miles away and took Arriviello into custody. Arriviello faces several felony charges, including malicious shooting into an occupied vehicle, maliciously causing bodily harm to another with intent to maim and use of a firearm while committing a felony. Arriviello remains jailed without bond at the New River Valley Regional Jail, officials told Fox News Digital. He is scheduled to appear in court Sept. 29. State police have not said what led to the alleged road rage encounter or whether investigators recovered a firearm from Arriviello’s Mercedes-Benz. The Jeep’s driver was also cited for reckless driving, but authorities did not identify the driver. SEE IT: DASHCAM SHOWS FLORIDA TROOPER CHASING ALLEGED STREET TAKEOVER SUSPECT AT 140 MPH North Carolina Medical Board records show Arriviello has been licensed as an emergency medicine physician in the state since 2010 and has no public disciplinary actions listed against him. The records list Arriviello as the owner of Family Urgent Care in Monroe. articles.title: Firefighters make progress against Reno wildfire that has destroyed dozens of homes, thousands still under evacuation orders
articles.summary: The Hawk Fire was 27% contained as of Monday afternoon, but still posed a threat to some neighborhoods.
articles.body:
Firefighters on Monday made significant progress against a fast-moving fire near Reno, Nev., that had burned dozens of homes and had threatened to spread into more neighborhoods earlier in the day.

The Hawk Fire, which began on Saturday, grew to more than 15,000 acres as it was fueled by strong winds and rugged terrain that impeded efforts to keep the blaze from spreading to residential areas over the weekend. More favorable conditions allowed firefighters to largely stop the spread of the blaze and achieve 27% containment, officials said.

"The threat has diminished significantly," Pete Briant, a division chief with the Reno Fire Department, said during a press conference Monday afternoon.

Firefighters have largely been able to eliminate the threat to communities along the fire's southern perimeter, which has allowed some residents who were evacuated from the area to return to their homes. As of 2 p.m. local time Monday, 23,000 people were still under evacuation orders and another 40,000 were under evacuation warnings, officials said.

The fire continues to pose some danger to neighborhoods along its northern perimeter, where fire crews have still not been able to establish any containment.

So far, authorities have confirmed that 32 homes have been destroyed by the blaze, though that number is expected to increase, Chief Richard Edwards of the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District said Monday afternoon.

Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency on Saturday, urging residents to "remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials." Nearly all schools in Washoe County were closed Monday as a result of the fire. The Washoe County Sheriff's Department has also ordered dozens of road closures in the area and partially shut down a major highway north of the city.

A total of seven injuries have been reported — four civilians and three fire personnel. There have been no reports of serious injuries or deaths caused by the fire.

Authorities said the fire was caused by humans , but have not provided specifics on how it started or whether it may have been lit deliberately. That matter remains under investigation, Edwards said.

County officials said earlier Monday that more than 700 personnel were actively working to contain the fire, including 14 fire crews, 95 engines and 10 helicopters. They reported that firefighters had "made progress" in keeping the blaze from spreading despite "extreme fire behavior" fueled by strong winds, high temperatures and extremely dry brush in certain areas.

Extreme fire conditions are expected to continue for at least the next 48 hours, which could allow the fire to continue to spread to the northeast and northwest, potentially into neighborhoods north of Highway 395.

Authorities have not said how many structures have been burned so far.

Reno is the second city in the western United States this month to see homes lost and mass evacuations due to out-of-control wildfires. In early August, a trio of fires burning simultaneously near Spokane, Wash., forced 60,000 people to evacuate, destroyed more than 800 homes and caused in excess of $1 billion in damage.

Across the U.S., there have been more than 50,000 wildfires that have collectively burned more 7.8 million acres of wildland so far this year. That's already substantially more than the average number of fires and acres destroyed annually over the past 10 years with more than four months left in 2026, according to the National Interagency Fire Center.

Cari Kiefer, a Reno resident who shared a video of her family's home burning on social media, told the Associated Press that she and her husband rushed to save whatever possessions they could before the blaze consumed their house.

"I kept looking outside and the flames just kept getting closer and closer every time I looked," Kieffer said. "I was like, we gotta go like now."

After the fire had passed through, only a scorched basketball hoop remained standing in the spot where their home once stood.

"I woke up this morning and just started crying — all my kids, they lost everything," Kieffer said Sunday. "We lost all our stuff. Everything we own is gone."
